Conducted between 7 June 2026 and 15 June 2026

Published: October 2026

Executive summary

From 7 to 15 June 2026, 3 officials from the Country Policy and Information Team (CPIT) carried out a Fact Finding Mission (FFM) to Bangladesh. The purpose of the mission was to gather information from a range of sources about the political situation since the July 2024 uprising and the resignation of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in early August of the same year. Below is a summary of information provided by sources.

The political situation has stabilised and generally improved since the July 2024 uprising, following the interim government period and the formation of a Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government following the February 2026 elections. Political parties, journalists, civil society organisations and human rights groups reported greater freedom to operate, express views and engage in public debate than under the previous Awami League (AL) government. However, concerns remain regarding corruption, police accountability and effectiveness and the limited implementation of wide-reaching reforms proposed following the uprising.

The BNP, Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI), National Citizen Party (NCP) and other political opposition groups are able to organise, campaign, protest and criticise the government. Political violence continues to occur, but is generally localised and most often relates to disputes over local influence, business interests, resources and political control at the local level. Sources described the 2026 election as generally peaceful and significantly less violent than previous elections and noted that political violence has reduced since the election.

The AL remains banned and public hostility towards it as an organisation remains, due to human rights abuses committed during its period in power and the events surrounding the July 2024 uprising. Low-level AL supporters who were not associated with corruption, violence or repression are generally described as able to remain in their communities. However, those openly expressing support for the party may face harassment, societal hostility or violence. Some former AL members have aligned themselves with other political parties, relocated within Bangladesh or left the country.

Most people arrested on politically motivated charges under the former AL government have been released and most cases have been withdrawn. Police sources stated that more than 21,000 politically motivated or false cases have been withdrawn and that reviews of historical cases remain ongoing.

Large numbers of AL politicians, activists and officials continue to face criminal proceedings relating to alleged actions during the former government and the July 2024 protests. Cases are proceeding through both the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) and the ordinary courts. Some prominent individuals have been granted bail and released, while others remain detained pending trial.

Introduction

Background

This report contains the (approved) notes of interviews with sources during a fact-finding mission (FFM) to Bangladesh.

It does not provide advice on handling particular types of protection claims. For this, see the Bangladesh: Country Policy and Information Notes.

The FFM was conducted in Bangladesh between 7–15 June 2026 by 3 officials from Country Policy and Information Team (CPIT), with support from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO). The team visited Dhaka.

Purpose of the mission

The purpose of the mission was to gather accurate and up-to-date information from a range of sources about the political situation since the July 2024 uprising, primarily on the treatment and activity of different political groups. Additionally, the mission sought to gather accurate and up-to-date information from a range of sources about law and order since 2024, the status of historical politically motivated arrests and the progress of cases involving alleged human rights abuses under the Awami League government.

See the Terms of Reference (ToR) for topics identified as relevant areas to explore.

Research standards

The FFM was undertaken with reference to the EU [European Union] common guidelines on (Joint) Fact Finding Missions: a practical tool to assist member states in organizing (joint) Fact Finding Missions, November 2010 (EU Guidelines 2010), and CPIT’s internal guidelines for conducting FFMs.

Identification of sources

The FFM team sought to interview a wide range of informed sources (interlocutors), including members of non-government organisations, government officials, and academics. Sources were identified primarily by desk-based research and in consultation with the FCDO.

The sources contacted and interviewed are those that the FFM team were able to identify as relevant to the mission’s ToR. But, as with any FFM, factors including time constraints and availability of sources mean that the list of sources consulted and information provided are not exhaustive.

That a particular source was interviewed and the notes of the interview have been included should not be taken as endorsement of that source or the information provided. Rather, all sources and information provided need to be critically assessed and considered against other publicly available material.

See List of sources.

Arranging and conducting interviews

The FFM team met 15 sources, consisting of 24 people in 15 face-to-face interviews.

All interviews with sources were conducted in English.

At the start of each interview the FFM team explained the purpose of the mission, including that the notes of the interview may be published in a report on the GOV.UK website and the sources would be able to review the notes before publication.

See FFM introductory note.

Notes of interviews/meetings

The FFM team took notes of all meetings, which were then sent by email to the sources for review and approval. This email explained that if a source did not respond within a specific deadline, then CPIT would assume that the source was content with the notes as sent to them.

Of the 15 sources, 12 approved the notes with a number making amendments to the original drafts. 2 did not respond. One did not agree to publication of the notes.

One source provided footnotes when making amendments to the original drafts.

All sources are described and referred to according to their preference.

Terms of reference

A ‘Terms of Reference’ (ToR) is an outline of what the FFM seeks to cover. Prior to the FFM, the following topics were identified as relevant areas to explore. Note: the FFM focussed on the country situation since July 2024.

FFM introductory note

Aim of the fact-finding mission

The purpose of our visit is to obtain accurate and up-to-date information on the political situation since June/July 2024. We would like to meet with you to fill gaps in our knowledge on this subject.

The fact-finding mission team will be made up of 3 officials from the Country Policy and Information Team (CPIT).

About CPIT

CPIT is part of the UK Home Office, the government department responsible for immigration and asylum. We collect country information through both desk-based research and in-country visits.

The reports CPIT produce are published online. They are used primarily to assist UK immigration officials and judges involved in the asylum and human rights decision-making process.

More information about the CPIT’s range of products, including reports of other Fact-Finding Missions, can be found on our website: Country policy and information notes - GOV.UK (www.gov.uk).

Format of the fact-finding mission

During our visit we will be meeting a range of sources who can provide an informed view on the issues of interest, which are listed below.

We intend to take notes of the meetings. These notes may be made publicly available on the GOV.UK website and/or used in litigation proceedings.

However, we will not publish any information you provide if you do not consent. If you prefer that the information is not made publicly available, this will be respected.

We will provide you with an opportunity to review/amend the meeting notes to ensure they are an accurate reflection of our discussions. We will also ask you how you wish to be cited in our final report. If you are not willing to be named individually, you can choose to be identified in more general terms. Examples include: by the name of your organisation or department (‘an official from the Department of Health’), or by your occupation (an ‘academic’ or ‘journalist’).

Interview notes

Interview with National Citizen Party (NCP) Member of Parliament

Date: 07 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Navid Nowroz Shah; 3 CPIT officials; 1 FCDO official

How has the political environment has changed since 2024?

Basically, all of us know Awami League (AL) and the Interim Government (IG) era governance struggled a little, especially the police force. There were a lot of people involved who were chosen by the previous regime that remained in the police force. A lot of people lost their faith and trust in the police force, and they struggled to carry on in their regular functions. As trust was lost, people hesitated to reach out to them when anything urgent arose. At the time, we thought when the elected government took over things would change and improve, of course things have improved a little, but the AL have increased again nowadays which is an issue.

The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), the ruling party, are favouring AL ‘goons’. They are in the judicial process and are on trial, but they are favouring them and [AL members] are coming out of prison and obtaining positions even though their activities are banned. But still they are released and committing vandalism. That is the whole situation in relation to law and order after the July [2024] uprising.

In terms of the power of people, I should say, people understood they had power. The government, police and other forces are behaving better than previously so there has been positive change and they are respecting people. It is better than ever, but we have a lot to do as political party, as general citizens, as a nation, we are working towards that.

What about the impact on your political party and how you operate, as opposed to previously during the Awami League government? Is there more freedom to operate now?

Of course, during the Awami League era opposition parties could not operate at all and now it is quite ok, the political situation is very normal. The government is doing its job, they do make some mistakes, but we are fulfilling our responsibility [as opposition] in criticising the government. There have been some ‘corrective politics’ happening and a little bit of unfair pressure from the government. There have been some incidents in the past 100 days, 6 or 7 people have been arrested for criticising the government which has been a negative, but still the situation is better than before. The government is not autocratic yet, we can still say that things upset us.

There was an incident before Eid [2026] in Jheinaidha district which is in the southern part of the country, 3 people from the NCP were attacked by BNP people but the police arrested NCP members and kept them in jail during Eid. Everyone knows it was a fake case and a political arrest from the government. In general, it is a better situation but it is not up to the mark we expected after the uprising, we were not expecting unlawful arrests. So many lives were lost in the uprising, and they sacrificed themselves for freedom of speech and politics.

What is the new government’s commitment to the recommendations on reform and the July Charter?

It is a huge blow, the government is not interested in implementing reforms. During the whole reform process, over a year the interim government collated opinions from civil society and politicians and then they proposed the July Charter. Even though there was dissent from BNP, it was still went to a referendum and the ‘yes’ vote won. The people voted in favour which the government has totally ignored. In the last 100 days, there has been no sign of any reform or issue in favour of reform. This has been a huge upset to people who voted BNP and voted yes to the July Charter, they have been betrayed from what was proposed in the election mandates.

One example of this is the government refraining from their commitment on a judicial secretariat. In the BNP election mandate, they vowed to implement an independent judicial secretariat but after forming the government they did not do that.

That’s a very big upset for the whole nation but still we are voting in favour of reform. But we are still not taking to streets or protesting because after almost one and a half decades the elect[ed] parliament is functional. We have 6 MPs and 2 more female MPs who are also advocating in parliament for reform. But, if the situation continues there will be no other option than taking to the streets because this is the whole point of the uprising, people want change.

What the main aims and objectives of your party?

We are trying to do proactive politics. Our main agenda is reform and secondly employment, as the uprising started from need of employment.

Recently, we presented the shadow budget, before [the] official budget, if we had been in power what we think the budget should have been. We outlined what should be done. It focused on reform, employment and investment. Our focus was on those 3 points. We have shared it with the government, and we will see if they take our recommendations as people need jobs. The whole world is seeing inflation; there is chaos everywhere. Jobs are the most important issue. All other policies will come later as ideology doesn’t matter if you don’t have a job and can’t feed your family. We need skilled workers and levelling up for the youth. We have a huge youth population and they should be skilled. Many workers are not skilled, and they make low wages compared to other countries. Our whole population should be skilled, even if they go abroad to work, they would be able to send back more money if they got more wages and a higher salary.

What is the profile of your supporters/members - who is voting for your party?

Mostly the youth. During the election, we had a hard time convincing the older population as we are very young. The older generation have difficulty trusting the youth because they think they have more experience. Due to the changes, civil society, senior politicians and senior activists have joined [our] party but it is mostly youth. Most of them are not voters yet which was a problem we faced during the election. I visited my local district Comilla [Cumilla, Southeastern Bangladesh], we had a political event within the upazilas [administrative districts]. 70% of those who willingly came to meetings and assemblies are under 18 and they have a huge interest in our party, think we are talking sense and could represent them well. From our perspective, we have to be in field for the next 4/5 years and then we will see if we have their votes.

Have you got national presence or are there certain areas where you have more support?

Mostly, in Dhaka and urban areas. Our whole movement is based on universities, schools and colleges. Our supporters are more from urban areas. The rural areas are run by local senior citizens so we have to take some more time to reach them and gain trust but we [are] working on that.

Can you explain your alliance with Jamaat e Islami (JeI) and how that is working?

Basically, ideologically we are totally different. From the beginning, our politics has been centrist beliefs, people in our party are very progressive, I am a centrist liberal, but we have to follow the alliance due to our reform agenda. We had discussions with other parties, we felt that the BNP is anti-reform and want to use the previous structure to rule the country. They are better than the AL, for sure, and they have good intentions for people but we can’t rely on intention, we need change in government structure. So, the alliance is ideological, we have an alliance based on the need for reform, that is it.

We are operating separately as single party[ies] as we have to spread out across Bangladesh. Jamaat is already established. Our point of common interest is reform only and we openly criticise Jamaat in talk shows and across social media, we criticise on issues such as women in power and religion. We are in an alliance for reform because we haven’t seen any improvement on that front yet, we will see how it goes over next few years. There are local government elections next year, we are preparing for those on our own. We want our political party to win, if we see that to beat BNP we have to form alliance, we might or we might not.

During the election period there was some reporting on inter-party and intra-party violence - did you experience this or were you aware?

Many incidents happened but this has been one of the fairest elections in the history of Bangladesh. There were some incidents, in specific seats. If the election was totally free and fair, then maybe the BNP wouldn’t get 200 plus seats but would still form the government. Maybe with around 20 or 30 seats. Maybe the BNP did some election engineering, but it was a free and fair election. There were some incidents, but there were very few. Still, we expect none to happen, but compared to other elections, there were very few.

Since the elections have there been any violent incidents?

Yes, there have been violent incidents, political incidents. It has calmed down and has not got worse yet. Most incidents are intra-party, BNP people fighting as they are a huge party. Of course, in the absence of the AL they are trying to control local powers and are fighting amongst themselves. There are few inter-party incidents, I already mentioned the one in Jheinaidha where 3 members of my party were arrested. There have been a few other incidents with the BNP. For example, there was an incident where the BNP vandalised the place where we arranged an assembly and are targeting top leaders and attacking them, so that we can’t expand our party across the region. It’s alarming, the BNP are showing signs of autocracy, I hope they will get over it soon.

What about the police response to those types of incidents?

It is a sad reality that the police are favouring government, as always. We protested during the Awami League era and the police were in favour of the Awami League. Whenever we try to say anything against the government, the police have not improved. However, the situation is not the same under the BNP, the BNP is showing some promise, so still we are hoping and waiting. It is still only 100 days, so we are ready to give that time to the government, but we are doing our job as an opposition party. It is early days, there hasn’t been much time to implement institutional reform, we are ready to give that time to the government.

Regarding the July 2024 protests and the arrests that took place then, are you aware of cases of people being prosecuted or still detained?

Most cases have been withdrawn and no one has been detained. Some cases are pending but they will withdraw cases soon, so we hope for no problems.

Are people able to protest now against whatever they want? Is there freedom to protest, to assemble?

Yes, people can protest now, the situation is okay, but as I mentioned there have been a few incidents. The general people can protest, and the BNP are not putting any pressure on police, but if we as a party organise a protest or assemble, some people have been attacked by the BNP. But the situation is not that bad, so let’s see how it goes.

Does the police response depend on the topic of the protests, for example land rights versus political?

No, I don’t think so, there is freedom to protest, it’s ok for now. But if you specifically criticise the prime minister then the situation gets worse, which we saw during AL as well; you could criticise the AL but not PM Sheikh Hasina, they made her a god-like creature. A few people have spoken out against Tarique Rahman, they have been arrested, but this is not the general scenario. We hope that this government will allow freedom of speech because the government knows what happens if freedom of speech is actually attacked.

Can BNP members now operate freely? Does it differ at local or national level?

The situation is ok, I think. There are very few incidents but not like before.

Is there any more information you are able to give in relation to the political situation now?

If I could say one thing, the whole political situation is better than during the interim government and during the AL era. However, this was not the expectation after the July [2024] uprising. There were millions on the street in July [2024] and so many lives lost in order to build a new country. The situation is not that promising yet, we are not sure that the government is intending to bring that positive change. It is better than the AL and BNP is a better party, but they are unsure of the reform needed which is what the people wanted. As I mentioned, it is better, so we can still hope, even as the opposition we still have hope.

Interview with a Political Analyst at International NGO

Date: 8 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Political Analyst at International NGO; 3 CPIT officials

Can you give some background on your role within the organisation and current priorities?

I have been with [NGO] since 2012, the team works directly with the political parties, not with other organisations. The project started in 2011, and between then and 2024 only the AL has been in power. Now we are working in a situation where the AL it totally out of the political space.

Our objectives have been to support political parties to be more democratic, have a more inclusive organisation, promoting women [and] youth participation and also to help parties to have more horizontal and vertical dialogue, to have more communication across different tiers of their organisation. We help parties to build their own training units at district level. We help them build tools for conflict mitigation at district level. Around the election we helped them to build teams for campaign management, poll watcher management, and candidate training. The aim was to provide support to all but there was a different approach in relation to the party in power and others, according to party priorities. We worked with Jamaat e Islami [JeI] until 2013 but then JeI was pushed out of the political space until 2024, now we have again started working with them.

Since after the 2024 uprising, we have been working with the new political parties such as NCP [National Citizen Party], GOP [Gono Odhikar Parishad] and loosely with some left-wing political parties and continued work with BNP. However, until July 2024 our core work was with the AL and the opposition BNP, with some engagement with Jatiyo Party. Work with Jatiyo Party is currently on hold.

[Part of our work is] promoting political cooperation and tolerance. We have multiparty forums engaging all major political parties and they work together as a team. There have been wonderful activities and examples of working together (cooperation across parties) in 22 districts. We have many examples of co-operation, for example when police were harassing BNP members previously or if they were arrested, AL counterparts helped them to get bail or protect their properties from vengeance.

The same happened in August 2024 when the mobs were torching AL properties, BNP’s local leaders were protecting them and their properties, and this was due to their connections in multi-party forums. Multi-party forums work together to solve community problems (ie water, health, drainage). When they work together the problems get solved quicker.

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

Our program has changed.

What was your experience during the election period in relation to election-related violence?

There was no widespread political violence during the pre-election period. We promoted peaceful election processes across the parties. It was a realisation from opposition parties that if there was violence BNP, JeI etcetera would be the losers. We shared survey data with decision makers and campaign managers in political parties which found that 92% of people would not vote for a party engaged in violence. This enabled an understanding at grass roots levels.

We had a response system - if we suspected any violence was bubbling then we would contact the political parties to get them to internally resolve. We were afraid that the interim government (IG) was not really prepared to handle the situation if there was widespread violence. The IG control of police was weak, and police morale was low but because participating political parties did not want violence, it was one of the most peaceful election periods. Our interventions also helped to prevent political violence.

Has the newly elected BNP government implemented any recommendations from commissions formed under the interim government – if so, what?

They have said they will proceed based on their manifesto and their own reform agenda rather than those under the July Charter. The IG had a long list of recommendations including 9 reform commissions prior to the July Charter and although not all were taken forward, significant ones were. The BNP have backtracked saying they will apply their manifesto, not the July Charter. We are still waiting to see if they will apply their manifesto. They claim some progress against the core commitments, for example about Family Card distribution (which they are piloting). In many other areas however, for example freedom of expression and of media, we are not seeing much movement towards reform, although it is still early in the new government.

Are members of political parties able to freely express themselves? Are they able to organise/attend demonstrations?

Yes, there has not been a widespread protest. In general, JeI and NCP, they have been calm, they are not protesting that much. However, we have seen them protest when they want, and some ‘soft’ protests. So far there is no evidence that they have been oppressed.

We are seeing a rise in AL rallies outside Dhaka, and they are sometimes turning into violent exchanges with BNP activists locally. Not many but at least a few recently, last week.

What has been the police response to AL rallies?

In Dhaka, AL rallies have been on a small scale because police disperse them quickly. The AL are now choosing different areas, for example in rural areas where there are 3 police officers and 1,000 people rallying.

However, where there has been violence, there have been some arrests of AL people.

On that matter, police arrests after August 2024, we are seeing that police behaviour is a continuation of the misuse of power that they were using under the AL. Police behaviour did not change dramatically or improve.

Would police behaviour be politically motivated, i.e. acting on the behalf of the BNP?

Mostly officers will act on their own behalf. But they also need to show the new government that they are doing something, i.e. prove themselves. There is also the bribery culture in Bangladesh, we call it ‘police trade’, i.e. pay for release which has been going on as long as I remember, and it’s continuing.

Is that a systematic attitude?

Yes, it was during the AL. The BNP were picked up in a van for hours and were not even taken to the police station. Then they paid some money through their relatives for release. If they did get to the police station, then the rates would increase. So, victims try to negotiate as early as possible.

Have there been examples of post-election inter-party and or intra party violence, ie BNP/NCP/JeI?

It has not been widespread, and it has been low level, more disruption for example throwing eggs or stones or shouting at each other, low level violence.

Has there been any violence committed by the state under the new government?

No, there have been some arrests by law enforcement, but we haven’t heard about violence which we did hear of during the AL time.

Is there any update on those held for their actions under the Hasina regime? Are people still in custody? If so, on what charges and at what stage of the process are cases? For example, are cases proceeding towards trial?

Trials are ongoing, and we are observing a few AL leaders and some people who had an understanding with the IG and BNP government, the court accepted bail and they were released. When a court grants bail, there is always a suspicion that there is a behind the scenes understanding.

Selina Hayat Ivy, a prominent leader of the Awami League and the former mayor of Narayanganj City Corporation has been released. The AL leader Saber Hossain Chowdhury’s bail was fast tracked. He secured bail within 48 hours of arrest in October 2024.

However, most of the leaders who were arrested are still in custody and trials are moving forward and will be heard soon.

Has there been any accountability or justice in relation to police who were involved in violence during the protests?

No, it doesn’t seem to have been reported. Some policemen have been arrested but I have not seen any public article or news about what is happening with their trials, so it’s hush hush. Maybe there is something happening, but it is not publicly talked about.

Is there an update on those held on politically motivated charges under Hasina – do people remain in custody? On what charges? What is the profile of such people?

Most of those arrested have been released after August 2024, by early 2025, under the IG.

If members of the AL now experienced problems in their community, would they be able to seek protection from the police?

It’s unlikely but depending on the local context they may. It depends on the police officer himself and his intention, and the motive and intention of the local administration. Some may not want the trouble, in other areas it might be the opposite, so the context matters.

In the community, are AL supporters/members able to express their political opinion?

People in the local community know each other. Pre-election, JeI and BNP went to the AL leaders in their community and sought their support. Mostly, this was from the BNP and Jel but some[times] also NCP. So, most are safe due to negotiated deals and alliances with other groups. Safety and protection are one of the main reasons they did this. The direction from the AL out-of-country leadership was to not take part in the elections, but ordinary AL people realised they had to protect their businesses and futures by siding with other political groups.

There is no widespread persecution of AL people, they are generally safe. However, there are some that want to protest violently or be active in politics to demonstrate to Sheikh Hasina that they still support her and are doing something for her. It is those people who are getting into trouble.

Could someone re-locate to another area?

Yes, many have shifted to other districts, perhaps living with relatives. Many thousands moved, some have started to come back to their areas after the election although not all.

What is the role of auxiliary organisations (particularly student wings) in political parties?

The important ones are the student, labour, youth, voluntary and women’s wings. They work as ‘brotherly or sisterly’ organisations or wings. They are important as they provide significant mobilisation power to each party.

How closely affiliated are they to the main party or are they focused on their own priorities?

They are not. We have asked these questions, why is the woman’s wing not focused on women’s issues, why are you only carrying out party programmes, not really working as independent organisations. The party leadership decides who will be the top leaders of these organisations. Even Tarique Rahman will choose the leader of the student wing of [the] BNP, he is very fond of the student wing and he personally manages that, there are other leaders who manage each of the wings.

Has this influence remained?

The practice has not changed yet, I don’t think that with the old political parties this is going to change soon. However, JeI is different, they will not run theirs by senior leadership, their student organisation is quite independent, but their women’s organisation is kind of more dependent on the main leadership. The student wing is very independent and important for them, based in universities and they have town/city-based communities. Many of the current BNP and JeI leaders have track records of student politics from the student wings. Student politics is very important in Bangladesh.

Are they based in universities?

They have a presence in all educational institutions, and also in communities. [This information was added after the meeting The student wings have units in all administrative units of the country, i.e. city, municipality, ward, district, upazila, union, along with the university and college campus-based units.] They are students when they join these organisations, and there was a time when they would continue to be in the student organisation even after they finished. However it has changed, they no longer have members who are not studying in the universities, this changed around 2016/2017 onwards. AL and the BNP were the ones who decided to change that. [This information was added after the meeting This change is mostly visible in their campus units. For the units at the communities this is a work in progress.]

Does the AL student wing which was banned under the IG remain banned under the BNP?

It is still banned. The BNP has passed a law in parliament, so it is more solid now, previously it was just an order of the president, but now it is a law. When the AL is banned, auxiliary organisations are also banned.

However, AL’s exclusion from the political space is a high-risk factor for politics and could cause future instability in the country, which will not be good for our economic development. We are working on an analysis of AL’s pathway in the next year. They have a strategy plan for the next 12 months or so which includes flash mob kind of rallies in places beyond significant police control. They also have plans for participating in local elections, so if there is resistance from any of the parties, there can be violence at the local level, at grass roots level. Local elections when they happen, it is not nationally important, and the military are not involved at same level as national elections. Candidates would be billed as ‘independent’ candidates. It would be hard to resist AL candidates, but I fear there will be resistance from BNP and JeI especially. JeI because they are especially keen to gain local government influence.

So, to have an inclusive political process is a long-term desired scenario, and I think BNP has a very difficult task in their hands as a government. There is pressure from NCP and JeI to not allow AL to come back. We see that on the one hand the government have passed a law banning AL more permanently, at the same time we see they are not really strongly supressing AL at the grassroots. I’m not sure how much of it is planned, we are trying to assess. Is this a planned strategy to manage JeI? AL is always a fear-factor for JeI, so they can use it as a card to negotiate with JeI, so are they doing that? This is something we are trying to understand.

There are elections within lawyers’ associations (known as bar associations). Outside Dhaka, we see AL lawyers are winning in some places and there is not much resistance against that. They are not winning main positions but they are winning important positions within the bar associations. This could be part of the AL’s comeback strategy, as bar associations and social organisations have value in society, and it could help them to reintegrate into society. It could be part of their 1-year tactic, to gain space, and local elections might be another. The AL also has very strong online activism. Some activists who are not in Bangladesh are very vocal on Facebook, and those who are in Bangladesh are becoming more and more vocal every day.

Is the government interested in social media posts?

The AL had a tight control over social media, but the BNP does not seem to have such a strict control. Although there have been some arrests for expressing criticism against individuals such as the Prime Minister (PM), it was not widespread like previously. The PM and ministers have said that they believe in the democratic process and allow freedom of expression. Arrests of some activists, journalists, there are some issues, this is something to observe. If these kinds of arrests continue or increase, then the government statements will not match their actions.

Does your organisation hold any data on reasons for arrests?

We don’t but there are other organisations who have, so we do look at it. [We look at available data from other organisations and avoid duplication of efforts.]

It is still early in the BNP government to find out what’s happening [it’s too early to establish a trend]. It is very difficult to understand unless you have grown up in Bangladesh. There are lots of nuances that are difficult to understand from afar. Good to get the local level detail.

Interview with Advisor at Human Rights NGO

Date: 8 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Advisor at Human Rights NGO; 3 CPIT officials; 1 FCDO official

Advisor at Human Rights NGO: [Human Rights NGO] provides legal assistance to communities and human rights monitoring. I work on the forced migration portfolio, legal aid to refugees and human rights documentation.

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

I think the first thing is, if we are holding 2024 as benchmark, it has improved a lot in terms of stability. In terms of the interim government, there was uncertainty and we were unsure of how political progress would unfold.

There was a kind of stability and rebuilding of democratic means of government, for which the BNP and Jamaat e Islami (JeI) should be credited. We are still seeing the same kind of exclusion of [the] Awami League (AL) and AL members being accused of serious crime, or even low-level members accused of crime. So, in a nutshell, there have been improvements in terms of political mobilisation between the opposition and the government. A lot of it is still limited to parliamentary debates, which is good. There have been some street demonstrations, but the concerning thing is for law and order as a whole. We are seeing a slide-back to some of the characteristics under the interim government (IG), especially regarding mobs and religious conservative ideals.

Around the same time of the election, we saw a marked decrease in incidents, most stakeholders were fighting a political battle and were concerned about votes. Now this is not on the cards for another 4 or 5 years, we are seeing a return to concerning patterns that were endemic during the IG. Politically, it is a concern the way in which the BNP has consolidated power across the country. They have named administrators for the local government positions; these are elected positions. The lowest level is union, union chairman and upazila (sub-districts) and city corporations – they are supposed to have elected representatives since there haven’t been local government elections yet. These positions have been taken by the BNP. This is concerning in different ways as the BNP has shored up influence across different areas and has complete control over local budgets and local organisation. The process is less than transparent and there are legal black holes in regard to electoral laws. This is what happens when there are no elections, this situation is taken advantage of to put party men in positions of power. We are seeing a period of stability and of political consolidation.

Jamaat are more concerned at the way in which institutional assets are being handled, such as the Islami Bank, the biggest Islamic bank. Jamaat were in charge of the Islami Bank until the AL regime. Now the BNP have removed the head and replaced [them] with a BNP loyalist. The Islami Bank is the biggest bank in the country in terms of people who save money and it was the first Islamic bank. We are seeing that the BNP is starting to consolidate some of these private assets amongst party members, it is an institutional exercise but perhaps it is happening to a lesser degree than [under the] AL.

The other significant thing is the growth of the NCP after the election, they absorbed a number of political parties, and they are focused on building ground strength across different districts. Their numbers have quadrupled since the election. That would be my take on the political situation. There is stability, that’s a key thing to acknowledge. We are seeing stability we haven’t seen since 2023.

Would you anticipate the local elections to follow same pattern as the national election in terms of being (widely reported as) free and fair?

I think it’s going to be different. Local elections historically have low interest due to the ways in which the AL had consolidated power. There is going to be more interest now for people to run and independents to run. I’m not sure to what extent it will reflect how the 2026 election unfolded. Primarily, BNP members now hold local government positions and have a degree of power in districts they never had before. Historically, the BNP is not as big of a mass party as the Awami League, which had this expansive influence, so I’m not sure how that will reflect in the elections. I am certain that there will be allegations from the opposition about lack of transparency, that much is for certain. In terms of the role of the election commission, positions have been politicised similar to the Bangladesh bank and other governance bodies. Statutory positions and constitutional bodies are now under the influence of the BNP or BNP-leaning men, so there is fear that it might not turn out to be as good as the 2026 general elections.

You referred to a slide towards mob justice. During voting, there was pre-election violence, how does that compare to now and what are you seeing regarding political violence?

I think one of things prior to the elections which was of concern was around the formation of mobs, but they were fragmented, not systematic. The biggest mobilisation was against shrines, Sufi shrines, or against Muslims or groups of followers who didn’t follow strict Islamic rules. We have documented that 98 shrines were decimated, destroyed or looted, these represented the biggest systematic formations of mobs. Beyond that, the formation of mobs also was due to the perception around lack of security and law enforcement, where people thought it would be better for them to take the law into their own hands to seek justice rather than following procedure. Mobs were lynching people accused of theft, this was a big phenomenon for 6 or 7 months after the interim government took charge. There were community level watches and communities standing guard when the police were not there. There were a lot of organised assaults against people who may or may not have been thieves.

Returning to the most concerning statistics, 56 or 57 individuals in the last 3 to 4 months have been subjected to mob beatings. A large chunk of that is against individuals accused of sexual violence, it is one of the biggest things now. Recently, there was the brutal rape and killing of child in Dhaka. They handed down the death penalty to the accused yesterday. It was a concerning development that the trial ended in 6 days. The public sentiment was such that if the government didn’t bow down to populous demand there would be consequences.

It is a serious concern, a document from BLAST shows 2 incidents of individuals killed in mob beating, one an hour from Dhaka and one in the north of the country, two young men publicly beaten to death after allegations of sexual assault. These types of crimes are now being leveraged as an excuse to form mobs and do justice on perpetrators, and some may be wrongfully accused. Time and again police are unwilling or unable to deal with mobs. I would stress on the unwilling part more, because we have seen instances where police can disperse large crowds, but they simply do not engage anymore because of the public sentiment toward law enforcement. During the interim government confidence was shattered. If there’s anything unpopular or not public sentiment, they won’t show up or they will show up after and say [they] couldn’t get involved due too many people.

To clarify; is it that law enforcement won’t engage until the very end or will they let an incident happen and come in later?

So law enforcement is not going to engage until the very end, they let the crime happen then come in later. We have seen a rise in religiously driven mobs. Recently, we saw a mob target a Hindu school teacher who had talked about evolution in classrooms and made a comment around the loud call to prayers. He had a massive mob against him. Thankfully, he was not hurt but he was handed over to the police. The idea is that after 2024, there is a lot more emphasis on populism on all sides of the political spectrum than ever before. The government won’t make an unpopular decision.

As a legal aid organisation, this demand we are seeing now around ‘fast justice’ is really concerning. It’s a sliding scale. The trial we followed, the rape trial, there was nothing there, it was incredibly problematic how this trial operated. If any high court was to hear this appeal, they would likely acquit him. He had no chance to bring up witnesses or to question the prosecution. That again is a concerning thing – the high court will indict people. It’s a big problem now, that institutions are thinking and acting in populist terms.

What has the police response been in relation to inter- and intra-party violence?

The biggest standout during the interim government in terms of political violence was intra-party from within the BNP. The BNP was fragmented during the Awami League, so when it resurfaced there were a lot of cases. Most of the deaths from political violence were within the BNP. A lot of the pre-election violence within the BNP has dissipated. Now we are seeing some, again quite low numbers for Bangladesh, of inter-party political violence. Sometimes there will be skirmishes with political leaders. The NCP leader was subjected to attacks, heckling and the throwing of eggs from BNP members/supporters. There were no big clashes between student wings which was previously common. The AL and BNP student wings were not clashing violently on streets which is big positive. Student politics and violence has subsided over the past 2 years and a big reason for that is the starting up of student union elections. When democratic pathways are opened, violence goes down. A lot of violence now is around localised issues around land grabbing and control over resources and using that in terms of political rhetoric to mobilise support.

After the election, there were documented incidents such as the sexual assault of a woman who voted NCP being turned into political ball game. It was said that the BNP was enacting sexual violence against the opposition. Most political violence is also located in areas where Jamaat and NCP have members of parliament. Obviously that struggle is between BNP-led administration, placed in different stages/areas of local government, and members of the opposition. We have been seeing skirmishes in Chuna, where Jamaat or NCP won.

What about state perpetrated political violence, what is the situation now?

Violence against members of the Awami League hasn’t changed. The expectation from the Awami League was that after the BNP came to power they would reintegrate into society but that hasn’t happened. The BNP is less firm around AL reintegrating but still as firm as the interim government in terms of ensuring the Awami League remains heavily persecuted and the public sentiment hasn’t stopped. The public has anger (justifiably) against those in a position of power who committed serious crimes. We are seeing some ridiculous results of that. For example, the 23rd Chief Justice has been behind bars for 2 years now. First and foremost, he was aligned to the party but the biggest problem with him wasn’t that he was present during the shootings at the July [2024] protests, it was that he was the architect of, or credited with, the changes to the constitution which benefited the Awami League and he is being punished for that.

There are a lot of individuals remaining behind bars, but they have not engaged in crimes. Not to say they weren’t engaged in crime, but they are not in prison for the crimes they have committed. Awami League activities remain banned, and members continue to leverage random acts of violence, but there is no indication of some of those acts taking place. The biggest action, in terms of state action against AL and members, or those with any kind of affiliation, is that they have been removed from any bureaucratic position during the interim government.

There were big numbers of arrests/detentions of AL personnel reported in the media to start with. What’s the situation now?

I think prior to the elections, there were staggering numbers of arrests under the Anti-Terrorism Act. Many were arrested arbitrarily, there were around 15,000 every month, which led to the massive overcrowding of prisons. This is not happening anymore. A big reason for this is the end of the joint security operations, Devil’s Hunt [brought in by the IG to maintain law and order and address mob violence[footnote 1]] and then Devils Hunt 2, which were used to formally round up AL members across the country.

We are still seeing individuals getting detained under the Anti-Terrorism Act, but there has been a noticeable decrease of that. There haven’t been any high-profile arrests since the arrest of the previous Speaker [in April 2026], who has been bailed, but I don’t think that the BNP is targeting high profile individuals. However, they retain the capacity to do so under the Anti-Terrorism Act.

If an arrest warrant was issued under Hasina’s rule for charges against the BNP or JeI, a politically-motivated arrest warrant, would that still be acted upon?

There were a number of false cases dismissed during the IG period. They did a whole exercise where a significant number of cases against these individuals were dismissed. There was obviously a procedure to go through to dismiss cases depending on the stage of the case and the judge etcetera.

There were a number of individuals who have cases against them but they are inactive and they are being not followed through. This is the same as the policy under the IG on cases that were politically motivated and enacted during the AL government. These are not prosecuted anymore. Cases are seen through. The person accused will appear at hearings and the case will run through and end, or the charges are dismissed.

Although it does depend of the charges/type of case, police cases can’t be dismissed. For example, if a criminal case was filed against me for murder, the police can’t show up to the judge and ask for the case to be dropped. There is a procedure to follow on certain cases, but the expectation [for politically motivated cases] is that it won’t amount to anything and the judge will close the case.

Is your organisation tracking arrests or do you have statistics on politically motivated arrests?

No, I think Odhikar does though.

You touched earlier on barriers to seeking protection, can you expand on that? For a political opponent, if they are struggling with societal violence, are they able to seek protection from the police?

The BNP now is very focused on rebuilding law enforcement strength. The police under the IG felt blamed for something, and that was not just their doing, but they were the ones with weapons on the street. There was justified public anger against the police. They did not understand that public sentiment, despite police officers being engaged in the killing of protesters. People did not see justice or action for that. We saw the police IGP [Inspector General of Police] was sentenced to 5 years in prison for acting as a state witness under Hasina, however people feel the police are getting off easy for their role during the July [2024] Uprising.

The police still feel as though the interim government humiliated them as a force; with the changing of the uniform, the constitutional reforms, the police reform commission. The recommendation of the commission proposed the implementation of the Police Commission Act (PCA), an independent body to look over the Ordinance Act of Police. However, the BNP has completely shelved this PCA, so it is not in the works anymore. The BNP wants the Home Ministry to have complete control over law enforcement, and they are starting to shield lower level individuals accused of crime. At best, what we will see is some of the officers, the big ones, being sentenced for the killing of protesters and extrajudicial disappearance. They may be sentenced to death, but it may not go beyond that.

The BNP feels it needs police on side to enact its will across the districts. To your question of political opponents, I don’t think the police is centralised enough under the BNP for this to be a concern yet. If someone far away seeks protection, there will be a police response, it is not as politicised as under the AL. It might get there if the BNP is successful. It has removed people from key police posts like the Inspector General, which are now controlled by police individuals who are BNP aligned. We might see it again in time.

Has there been any progress on the BNP government implementing recommendations from commissions set up during the interim government?

There has been negative progress. The BNP have done away with useful architecture the IG set up, like the HR [Human Rights] commission. They have scrapped the enforced disappearance law, but they are coming up with their own version of that but it’s limited in scope. With the NHRC [National Human Rights Commission] Act, they have been trying to push to expand the commission’s power but are shielding security forces. The NHRC can’t investigate cops or military. It is the same for the Enforced Disappearance Act, it is going through parliament now. It has been very watered down, the sections on proving a case are now much stronger. It is now going to take a lot more to prove that someone involved in law enforcement was involved in an enforced disappearance.

The BNP is interested in doing populist things and has successfully engineered public attention away from reforms. It has also not been easy under the circumstances with the Iran crisis, fuel crisis and the cost of living. These are crises the BNP need to handle.

The BNP did set up a constitutional reform committee in parliament, which is different from the interim government which recommended a constitutional council. The July Charter was cancelled by the BNP. The constitutional reform committee will be a committee of parliamentarians who will decide how to change [enact reform], but the NCP and Jamaat are not involved as they want the July Charter.

Beyond the constitution [reform committee], the reforms on anti-corruption, public affairs and women, none of the recommendations are being taken up. As the anti-corruption commission was repealed as well, we are back to how it was performing under the AL. Women’s affairs [commission] proposed a number of important changes to law and statutory bodies, but it has not been taken up.

It is important to note the reforms the BNP have done. They have kept some useful things proposed by the IG. They kept a lot of criminal procedure revision, the biggest of which was section 54 amendments. The Code of Criminal Procedure allowed for arbitrary arrest and now there are stronger accountability and safeguarding measures, which is a positive. The BNP have also retained changes to the Violence Against Women Act, which provides protection for witnesses, and have retained good language in other acts like the Trafficking and Migration Act.

They have retained most things but in terms of implementing most reforms, this has not been done, and they often point to the global crisis. Once the parliamentary session on budget ends [July 2026], the reform position will be picked up by the opposition.

Again, it is important that we acknowledge it has not been long, we have had 4/5 months of government. I think we should give them a bit more time before making a harsh assessment.

Can you expand on justice and accountability for previous human rights abuses under the Hasina government?

I think the biggest problem is that the BNP wanted control of the justice sector. They repealed justice reform acts that the IG set up. The control of the judiciary is back to party loyalists. This is significant as it allows the ministry to control which judges are assigned where, what bench. It allows the ministry to control proceedings in the High Court through the Attorney General. The biggest criticism is they have reverted back to [the] structure [that was in place] under AL.

There were elections across the Bar Association, which ended with a clean sweep of BNP men everywhere. From the Supreme Court to lower courts, they were elected. It will be a highly politicised court. We haven’t yet seen it, but I imagine if someone wants to file case against the BNP leader somewhere, I don’t think it will be possible with how the Bar Council is set up. They won’t let lawyers from different political parties practice without their consent.

Look how due process was completely disregarded in the rape case I mentioned earlier. It was a horrific case; however, we can’t live in a world where a trial ends in 6 days. The prime minister promised that the trial would end in two weeks. It is not his job to tell us how long a trial will last. It will get to point where public sentiment is ok with stripping due process. We do not see any organisations speaking against it as it is so sensitive. Our statements have been around following due process, and we haven’t criticised but it deserves criticism. It is nothing to celebrate, it’s shocking.

What is your organisation’s ability to practice and follow your aims and objectives under this government?

So far, it’s not been terrible. Obviously, under the AL, it was really difficult in terms of day-to-day operations. Our funding stopped, we were heavily scrutinised, a lot of our senior staff were targeted through online mobilisation against them, in particular our Executive Director. This changed during the IG. One of the reasons for this is that people in the IG were colleagues at one point in time.

The BNP has been sincere in their engagement with us across issues for the Human Rights Commission Act. They have been sincere in receiving recommendations, that forum exists. That did not happen previously. I’m not sure if they will follow up, but that forum exists now, which did not happen before. They have also worked with us around the Violence Against Women Act.

On the issues of torture and arbitrary detention, while the Special Rapporteur was here, the government were sincere in their engagement. In that regard, I don’t know how long it will last. We are able to work and do what we do without taking into account political sensitivity. We can critique government decisions in front of the minister, which we previously hadn’t been able to do.

What is the legal status of the AL student wing?

It is banned as a terrorist organisation.

Regarding freedom of movement, how does local politics play out? Can a low-level political opponent move to another area if they had problems with the local community?

Can they internally relocate? Yes. Political violence has not reached levels seen under the AL when we saw horrific persecution. Again, now that the BNP is in power, political opposition groups have to come to a status quo. Locally, we haven’t seen violence. A lot of this is contingent on how local elections turn out and if we see a return to political violence. Locally, political violence has decreased.

For example, members of the political opposition can relocate. It seems to be fine and is definitely possible. If they are AL, it could be a problem. They may be liable to arrest and extortion, in exchange for not being arrested. The AL situation is not good. Really low-level members are not being persecuted. Student politicians engaged in the student league and involved in violence have been targeted. However, we’ve seen over course of last 5/6 weeks, for example, in Ranpur (Jamaat controlled), a big political personality who was AL is still there. Individuals have either switched sides or have come to an understanding with Jamaat or the BNP. If public sentiment isn’t against individuals, they are generally left alone.

Some AL union level chairmen are still there as the public didn’t have that feeling of resentment, especially if they have not been accused of corruption. I’m not saying everyone who was AL and arrested deserved it. I’ve seen at a local level those persecuted had negative public sentiment against them. Many did abuse power for 15 years, they looted public funds and did commit different crimes. It has to be a restorative process, which we are perhaps not seeing now. At the local level, there is status quo.

If someone was a low-level Awami League supporter previously, despite the ban, can they express their political opinion?

The expression of political opinion does exist, and it is usually ok to do so. But you cannot express openly your support for the AL. If you openly voice your support for the AL, there may be backlash. There could be public mobilisation and violence. The sentiment against the AL has not eroded and the anger is still there. People feel the justice process has not been sufficient. There has been the symbolic death penalty of the former Home Minister and the former Prime Minister, but other than that no one has seen any justice.

nterview with Human Rights Support Society (HRSS)

Date: 8 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Saiful Islam, Program Officer; Saneequdrat Saqee, Program Officer; Abu Shadat Md Sayem, Monitoring Officer; 3 CPIT officials; 1 FCDO official

Can you give an overview of your roles within the organisation and your current priorities?

Saiful Islam (SI): We are not a registered NGO yet. In terms of our work, we rely on 15 national daily newspapers and other volunteer sources. We publish monthly, yearly and half-yearly reports and special reports. We fact-find state-sponsored violations and support victims. We are training young people over months and years on human rights mechanisms. They are working as watchdogs and activists, and we have over 1,000 volunteers and committees in 15 universities and districts. We understand that human rights education starts in school and we have also introduced a college campaign and human rights Olympiad [a human rights competition for secondary students].

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

SI: Nothing has actually changed much. Regarding HR [human rights] violations, enforced disappearance has nearly stopped – we only had one case (a month ago) since 2024, that is a huge development. Otherwise, it is the same. In some cases it’s a bit worse. Especially regarding societal violence, including mob violence and social conflict. Political conflict is also not decreasing – it is more or less the same. Regarding state-sponsored extrajudicial killing, that is a bit lower. Other state-sponsored violations are happening, detention, imprisonment and death in custody. Violations against women have increased to some extent. It is concerning that the reforms instigated by the IG have mostly been scrapped – HRC (Human Rights Commission), EDACT (Enforced Disappearance Act) have been scrapped. That remains a huge concern.

Regarding political violence, have you seen a difference between pre- and post-election?

Abu Shadat Md Sayem (AS): Violence spiked during the election. After and long before the election, the frequency appears normal. It normally spikes during election periods and without exception it happened with this election too. [This information was added after the meeting Generally, election-related violence remains high from the announcement of the election schedule until election day. Within a week after the election, the situation usually returns to normal. This is the common trend in almost every election in Bangladesh.]

Intra-party violence was more intense during the electoral period from 2014 to 2024, largely due to the limited participation of other political parties in the elections. Now there is a more democratic space, there is both intra- and inter-party violence as there is competition, particularly between JeI and the BNP after 2024.

But during the AL regime, elections were not participatory so there was less inter-party violence because there was limited competition. In many cases, particularly in the 2024 election, independent candidates were from the Awami League too.

During this election was there any violence between student wings? How aligned are they with the main parties?

AS: Election [violence] mostly affected areas accessible to the general public. In the student areas it remained ‘normal,’ so there was no exceptional violence during the election period. Generally, student wings are involved in disputes and occasional violence related to student union elections, control of residential halls, and campus influence.

What is the role of the auxiliary organisation (student wing) in political parties? How aligned are they with the main parties?

AS: Most of the parties have student auxiliaries, especially those aspiring to gain state power. Their first priority is to catch people at the university campus, as that’s where protests begin and spread. They always try to have their student wing in each university. AL had BCL [Bangladesh Chhatra League] etcetera.

Saneequdrat Saqee (SS): It is a common trend in our country.

Are there any specific membership requirements?

AS: Generally, any student can become a member of these student wings. However, if they don’t have proper linkage to their political leaders or funding from their family, they may not get an expected position in the main party after their time in the student wing. A person would have to have proper backing/support from their leader and in their locality. ‘Muscle power’ works too. All those things will help to get a role in the main party.

There are different ways of functioning, i.e. JeI have proper ranking in terms of their political posts, although personal influence, muscle power, and family background may still play a supportive role. All other parties rely on a political power structure from money, family linkage/power etc.

SI: Jubo League is more senior than the student wing BCL. Also, Judo Dal is senior to JCD [Bangladesh Jatiotabadi Chatrodal]. [CPIT addition: This is in reference to the hierarchy of different student wings. The Jubo League is a different youth wing of the AL, and the Judo Dal is a different youth wing associated with the BNP.]

AS: Mostly, the phenomenon we experienced in the campus during our student life was that many student leaders had married but did not say so, because there was a de facto rule not to get married. In order to stay in the student wing, or to get a good position, one should not be married, so they would not disclose if they were married, but it’s not the same in [the student organisation] Shibir.

SS: The concern is only about their studentship.

AS: Regarding age, there was no age limit, but they do say a student wing person should be a student, as far as I can remember. In reality, this is not the case. They have to attend lots of programmes, lots of rallies, and that’s why they cannot keep up with their studies. In practice, most of the senior wing leaders are not students, or they are waiting to take their exams for 10 years for example.

Regarding protests now, is there freedom of expression (FoE) and is there any police response to protests?

SS: In campus, most students will be forced to go to their main party protests. However, now that practice is a bit diminished. Now, people can protest, apart from the Awami league. But the police still deal with them the same way, ie tear gas, rubber bullets and batons. We have seen several cases.

SI: After 2024, the barrier to FoE has been reduced a great deal. During Sheikh Hasina’s rule, there were a lot of restrictions. But after, people could express their political dissent more freely than ever. This sometimes caused problems, such as mob violence. As the IG were not elected, all the political parties and people generally could express themselves freely. We did not see any examples of detention.

Since the BNP have come in, we have started to see some sort of barrier in this area, in relation to online bullying, fake posts and videos of opponents which have been widely used by all political parties (BNP, JeI, AL, all parties). So, we have seen some legal action taken against some people. For example, we have recently witnessed the arrest of someone who was an activist, who had a Facebook page covering the local news about many things, but he was criticising a parliament member. He was detained.

The Cyber Security ordinance passed under the IG is now the Cyber Security Act. If someone is malicious online, only the victim can file a complaint. The above case [involved] normal information about corruption. He was detained and then bailed.

Some advisors to the PM have spoken to say there should be some measures in place to control malicious content online. It does need to be addressed, but if we cannot define it specifically and objectively then it can be used wrongly. We have seen 2 cases [This information was added after the meeting a man called Hasan Nasim and a woman called Sawda Sumi were detained, both were bailed but that was after their case went viral on the internet.]

On the national level, political leaders are criticising each other, there is no problem. However, at the grassroots levels there have been some reports [that] it has been harder to criticise the government.

Do journalists and CSOs/NGOs operate freely under the new government?

SS: It is still in a good position – they can work freely. However, we should have received our registration from NGOAB [NGO Affairs Bureau] within 45 days of the application submission, it’s held with the ministry. In practice, we are still working.

Is there any update on those held for their actions under the Hasina regime? Are people still in custody? On what charges? At what stage of the process, ie proceeding towards trial?

[CPIT addition: These answers are in relation to those arrested during the Hasina regime, such as student protestors.]

SS: There are 2 types of cases, one from the army and one from law enforcement. They were mainly accused of human rights violations. Some of the accused were arrested but due to the ordinance [July Mass Uprising (Protection and Determination of Liability) Ordinance, 2026], we would expect them to get bail without charges as it’s a crime that is very hard to prove. Some of the main perpetrators got arrested, some fled the country.

During the July 2024 uprising, there were 1,200 killed, as documented. Most of the cases against the perpetrators were politically driven. To give an example, a person was killed in front of the police station on 5 August 2024 in Jatrabari. But when he filed the case, they wanted him to file the case against 200 unknown people and another 300 [person] list of former political members.

Which political parties went to the victims’ families to ask them to file against more people?

[This information was added after the meeting In most of the cases, BNP men convinced victims’ families to file cases.]

Is there an update on those held on politically motivated charges under Hasina – do people remain in custody? On what charges? What is the profile of such people?

[CPIT addition: These answers are in relation to those held for their actions under the Hasina regime.]

SS: Many are still in custody, but a lot of them have been freed.

SI: In bigger cases, it is hard from them to get bail. But less significant cases or smaller leaders, they are getting bail. The judiciary is still trying to separate who were the perpetrators and who were not.

[This information was added after the meeting These answers are in relation to those who were arrested for their actions during the Hasina regime.

Most of the political[ly motivated] cases filed during the Hasina regime were dismissed. Some of the major cases are pending, but the accused got bailed.

Major accused and arrested persons were leaders and supporters of both BNP and BJI [Jamaat] and their student wings.]

AS: The people who were arrested under the Hasina regime, most are free. Two who were on death row are now free.

SI: Those are believed to be false cases. In many cases, we saw witnesses against political leaders (former state witnesses, who later decided to defend the accused) abducted from the court area but later found in India. Many leaders were perpetrators, but not to the extent alleged. And the trial process was not clear and has been criticised.

[This information was added after the meeting when asked by CPIT to expand on the above example Shukhoranjan (Sukhranjan) Bali was a Hindu resident of Pirojpur whose brother was killed during Bangladesh’s 1971 Liberation War. He was initially listed as a prosecution witness in the war-crimes case against Delwar Hossain Sayeedi. However, Bali later said that he did not believe Sayeedi was responsible for his brother’s murder and agreed to testify for the defense instead.

On 5 November 2012, while on his way to testify before the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) in Dhaka, defense lawyers and witnesses alleged that Bali was forcibly taken away by plainclothes law-enforcement officers from outside the tribunal. Human Rights Watch called for an independent investigation into the alleged abduction.

Bali then disappeared and resurfaced in May 2013, when he was found in detention in India - about six months later.

According to statements later attributed to Bali, he told journalists and human-rights organizations that he had been abducted by Bangladeshi security personnel, detained and mistreated in Bangladesh, and then illegally taken across the border into India, where he was further detained. Human Rights Watch reported his allegations that he had been forced across the border and held in Indian custody.]

Are there any barriers to members of the political opposition seeking protection? I.e. a member of the Jel or NCP if they were being threatened by a non-state actor?

SS: There have been cases of giving protection but there have been cases where they have not, including during the election.

SI: You have to remember, in local police stations police are short on manpower, in many cases there are not enough police. Even if they are willing to provide protection, they don’t always have capacity. But we have seen the police provide protection.

In Dhaka University, members of Chhatra Dal (BCL) had put up malicious content online and then there was some mob violence (people in the crowd got a few punches in) and the victims were sheltered in the police station. They could deal with it because it was Dhaka but it depends on what the ratio is of people to police.

Under Hasina police would just shoot on sight. However, now they are showing restraint, both during the interim government and since. They are actively seeking to avert harming protesters and do not want to use force. If protesters are then attacked, then police have to either just react or leave.

AS: One phenomenon is that the BNP and JeI were [previously] aligned [allies].

Regarding lower-level issues, JeI is smaller than the BNP, so have less influence. Another aspect of conflict at local level is because of disputes at a local government level such as business tenders. In those cases, BNP are quite powerful and get the tenders. Where JeI has more influence, there is some conflict to get tenders but it’s mostly peaceful.

[This information was added after the meeting JeI is not regarded as a full political opposition and is not considered a significant threat to the government, as it had not yet posed a substantial challenge through protests, rallies, or other political activities.] If there is no conflict, the government will not react and there is believed to have some consciousness [cooperation] with the top levels of both parties due to their prior political coalition.

Is there police protection available for AL people who fear a person in their local community?

AS: Mostly, the police will give protection to those who have power and the police also give protection if a victim’s content is on social media. [If there is media attention] it is in the interest of police. Unless there is political pressure, the police won’t react against the AL, for example.

If someone was a vocal AL supporter, would they be at risk of societal violence?

AS: It has improved. There is a low possibility of mob violence against a person with a political profile, including AL. It was a bit more under the AL [more likely for societal violence to be perpetrated against a member of political opposition under the AL government].

SI: People who did not politically oppress others [under the AL government], they live in harmony. But people who did oppress, they faced a difficult situation during the IG. Some of them were charged with many cases, and many benign AL supports have also been arrested, but right now the situation has improved. So it depends on their past actions as to how they might be treated in the community.

An AL leader who highly oppressed opponents and grabbed lands illegally, he can’t enter the village right now, but many of my school friends, they were BCL members, they are still in the village, nothing has happened to them. They are fine as they weren’t oppressive.

If someone was being threatened in the community (i.e. an AL member) could they move to another area?

SS: Depends on their level of seniority. If they were not senior or popular/known they can move to another area, as many are, but those who are very known, they have to flee the country, many are living in Nepal, India, and western countries as well.

SI: We have also noticed in my constituencies in the northern part of Bangladesh, I have seen that there is business between JeI and BNP. The connections have been there for a long time, they have come to their understanding. Money is the big issue here.

Surveillance had gone down a lot since the AL. They would hunt opposition like criminals. 250-300 cases would be put on one person, they would detain people at funerals, weddings, etc, they would hunt opponents. But this type of surveillance and monitoring has reduced. During the IG and now, this strong monitoring has reduced.

SS/SI: The NTMC [National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre] its functions are paused.
