AS: After August 2024, the agencies faced problems. The previous government (AL) used those agencies for surveillance and forced disappearance. When they were dismantled by the IG, including the LIC [Lawful Interception Cell], their actions were reduced.

[This information was added after the meeting The LIC is a unit used for surveillance under the police. None of the surveillance infrastructures were dismantled. They are still there. Another is the NTMC. Their functionality is on hold for now.]

SI: During the past 15 years, they [the Awami League] have taken a lot of money from the country. They are now taking shelter in other countries, saying if they go to Bangladesh they will be mobbed, but right now we don’t have that problem, they will be passed to the police. People grab them and hand them over to the police, this is the situation. Nobody is willing to get involved in mob violence.

In general, they can go back to their community in Bangladesh. The situation is different for a criminal.

AS: There are two problems on what they might face in communities and a potential trial. However, now the trials for political leaders are quite transparent. We don’t know how the government will react to those people coming back, so the risk is still there, but perpetrators are hiding out in another countries. Is there any legal mechanism in other countries to hold those people accountable?

SI: In regard to the ICT, they were criticised but now they have been trained and they have more transparency than they used to have.

SS: Two days ago, someone at the top of the AL was bailed. Someone else is being bailed today or tomorrow and the Speaker was also bailed. So I think, broadly, the consensus in our country is to follow the legal process for justice. The current government needs to do that. If they successfully do that, it will move us forward a lot.

[This information was added after the meeting One AL member is Selina Hayat IV, former Mayor of Narayanganj City Corporation. She is expected to run for mayor again in the next city corporation election. Another one is Professor Abul Barakat, who was known for creating groundwork for the financial corruption done by the Awami League regime.]

Interview with Human Rights Activist and Political Analyst associated with Ain O Salish (ASK)

Date: 8 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Human Rights Activist and Political Analyst associated with Ain O Salish; 3 CPIT officials

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

Starting from 2024, there were 2 phases. Immediately after the escape of Sheikh Hasina and the fall of the Awami League (AL) government, there was a vacuum in the government and in the situation, particularly in law and order. The law enforcement agencies were in hiding; they were not on duty. I would say there was a huge scope [sic, spate] of criminal activities and acts of vandalism during that period, especially that 3 or 5 days when there was no government at all.

Initially, students took up the responsibility of taking control in the streets. The interim government (IG), its formation process was more or less democratic, and it consisted of consulting most of the political parties, but there was concern that it didn’t involve the AL. Most of the AL leaders were in hiding, and many left Bangladesh (and so could not contribute). There were less options. The formation was mainly led by the military, supported by civil society, students, and other organisations.

During that period, it seemed that Professor Muhammad Yunus might be the best option to lead, and gradually the law and order situation started to improve. One concern for us human rights activists and political analysts was the filing of thousands of cases against several thousand unnamed persons, mainly against leaders and activists of the AL, but many became very controversial because they involved some people who were not at all involved with those cases. There were other similar cases like that as well.

Gradually, the political situation started to improve, [including] the decision-making process. The IG appeared weak in controlling the overall situation because people were coming out to the street, different groups and different parties, demanding rights, so that was a big challenge initially for the IG. So, we saw a surge in arrests, that was a big concern for us. We were concerned about detention without trial, prolonged detention, refusal of bail, they were the main concerns. We received complaints about torture in custody as well, these [the numbers] were not that high but still, there were complaints about it.

One of the improvements was on enforced disappearance, that went down to zero under the IG so that was a big achievement. Still the number is very low, today there is only one suspected case. That is an improvement in the human rights situation. The number of extrajudicial killings also went down. But they are still happening, some extrajudicial killings.

There were some demands from students in particular about the ban of the AL. The government banned the activities of the AL, until the ICT resolves the case[s]. There are several cases against the AL and its leaders including Sheikh Hasina. However, making provision for the trial of one political party, this is a difficult idea of accusing a political party and punishing it, but the law is implemented which was concerning. We have concerns about the death penalty and procedural issues e.g. one tier of the International Crimes Tribunal of Bangladesh (ICT) is ignored.

[This information was added after the meeting cases in regular [Bangladesh] criminal courts pass through the trial court, then the High Court Division of the Supreme Court and finally the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. However, the ICT is in the status of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, and the appeals go to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court. Thus, one tier of the court is removed for cases in the ICT. This was the same when JI [Jamaat e Islami] leaders were tried in the ICT.]

AL activities were banned. However, some activists and leaders have tried to join demonstrations together, and in these cases the police have tried to arrest them. There are some concerns that the activists of the BCL cannot pursue their education, some AL professionals cannot carry out their profession, or regular activities.

There are suspicions of corruption regarding some advisors of the IG. They tried to declare a roadmap for election, and finally it was held in February 2026. When the election days were approaching, the government appeared weak and there was not much confidence in the government regarding whether they would be able to handle the election or not. The educated class in Dhaka were initially not confident that the election would take place, but it did. The violence was increasing in the approaching election period, so that was another big concern for us, the violence and whether that would disrupt the election, but again this didn’t happen and the election was peaceful.

The political parties participated in the election, but the quality of the election can be questioned because the AL were not part of the process. It can be argued that they have lost their right to participate but I personally think they should be given a fair chance to contest the election. My feeling is that if the AL was there, people would have rejected them so that would have been democracy.

Another big issue was the amendment of the constitution and the reformation of the whole government process. Those commissions set up under the IG were very important and had some good recommendations as well but mostly they were washed away and not implemented. The referendum process was arranged, but the system was difficult to understand for the common people. Some of the IG’s activities became very controversial, they were saying vote for one option. [This information was added after the meeting [The NGO Affairs Bureau] NGOAB, the regulatory body of the NGOs, called a meeting chaired by the Head of the Reformation Commission and advised the NGOs to campaign in favour of the referendum. They were asking for specific commitments about the number of people etc that we will reach.] They said we should advertise on Facebook for a ‘yes’ vote. In that situation, we had to give some commitments and just walk away from there. When the regulator calls and asks us to do something, we feel pressure. Similarly, they pressured private banks as well, saying they should advertise their propaganda for the referendum.

Finally, the ‘yes’ vote won. After the formation of the new government, the BNP were expected to be in favour of reform but the BNP, after coming into power, refused to implement the recommendations of the July Charter, the issues of the referendum. The BNP said they would reform, but not as per the Charter, they said ‘we will reform on the issues for which we gave our consent’ [notes of dissent did not progress to referendum]. So according to them, reformation is a continuous process.

After the installation of the new government, there was a long holiday of Eid and the situation appears, at this point, more or less peaceful. The law and order situation is improving.

As human rights activists, we have concern about arrests, detention without trial, prolonged detention, torture and mass arrests. Hundreds or thousands of people have been affected. Another thing we see from the past is that there is a long culture of torture, so that is a big concern for us. In the July 2024 movement, we saw a huge number of deaths, 1,400, that is the calculation of the UN. We want justice for all the issues and allegations of human rights violations but that should be a fair process. We want justice for the victims of the July [2024] movement. We want justice for the victims in the last 15 years and for the victims of today. That is the broad idea of human rights activists.

[This information was added after the meeting In the political ecosystem of Bangladesh, currently there are right, centre right and left [leaning parties] only and there is no centre left. This is an imbalance. There is a very slim chance of the inclusion of centre left in recent times. So this imbalance will continue. There are concerns about the rise of right-wing political groups. Attacks on Sufi shrines and attack on Prothom Alo and Daily Star offices are indications of this.]

In terms of the justice process for events surrounding the July 2024 protests, what has been the experience so far? Have there been trials?

There are some trials going on in the ICT and in the regular trials court as well. Our experience of the justice process is that it is very long and we cannot say that this process will be unbiased. There is always an indication that the judges are looking at the signals of the government and want to deliver a judgement that the government likes.

Another interesting point in the recent past is the apprehension that there will be huge attacks on religious and ethnic minorities after the escape [fall] of the AL government. The minorities are usually perceived as voters of the AL (although this may not be true). So that created some problems in 2024, immediately after Sheikh Hasina, but the situation calmed down. There was some misreporting in the Indian media about attacks on the religious minorities, particularly the Hindus, in Bangladesh. However, this was not correct. After 2025, during the largest Hindu celebration, we saw a number of attacks on Hindu people during that time. There was some violence on [against] the minority community. When the election was approaching, we saw an increase in violence on [against] minorities, but the situation has calmed down now. There are still some attacks, but not many, I’m not trying to normalise it, but it is less.

Another point of concern at the moment, which has added a new dimension to this aspect, is the winning of BJP [Bharatiya Janata Party] in West Bengal. This can also work as a pull factor for Hindus. There can be some attempt of pushing-in Muslims. This may result in communal tension on both sides of the border. Apart from these, many Hindus who are educated have property in India. Apart from that, this new development in West Bengal works as a pull factor.

Have those arrested during the July 2024 protests, i.e. students, been released?

They have been given an indemnity for all the protests, so that is another point of concern for some groups of analysts. The other school of thought is that the situation was one of mass uprising and therefore there was no choice but to proceed that way. If there is a change of law, a new government could change this indemnity and could arrange a trial of the students.

Have those charged under the Hasina government on politically motivated charges been released or are there people still in detention?

In the past, there were hundreds and thousands of cases under the AL against Jamaat and BNP, the political opponents. After the IG came to power, they dismissed most of the cases, though a few cases are maybe still pending.

If an arrest warrant was issued under the Hasina government against a political opponent (or perceived political opponent), would that arrest warrant still stand, would they take action on that?

No, they won’t be operationalised at this moment, because the cases are lifted so the warrant won’t work at this moment. We are seeing most of the BNP activists who were hiding to dodge the process, they are now mostly free so they are walking around the streets, participating in the political activities of the BNP and JeI. Their concern has gone away. But now we have this concern around AL activists.

People who made money through corruption or other means (AL), most of them have escaped from Bangladesh or they are hiding but activists who couldn’t manage to escape, they are getting harassed at this moment.

Are members of the political opposition able to seek protection if they are being harassed by non-state actors? If so what, and at what level – local/national authorities?

At this moment, the overall sentiment is against the AL and it is very high, so protection inside Bangladesh is a bit difficult. But they are managing things in an understanding with the BNP and JeI. After the change in the government, these things are working differently. This process of bribing shows us there is a mutual understanding that operates on the ground, between the activists.

Bribery, is that at local or national level?

On every level. One example is a Minister, Nasrul Hamid Bipu, who fled Bangladesh. He was managing big businesses during AL’s rule. It is alleged that former Advisor to the IG Ms Syeda Rizwana Hasan’s husband was managing Mr Bipu’s business. After Hasina fled, everything was cracked down upon, so the BNP have filled the vacuum. The AL had their own system of managing things, that is a parallel system. The BNP guys have stepped in and they are seeking assistance from the AL for business interests and illegal business, extortion, bribery etc.

Is there societal violence against low-level AL supporters now?

That is happening to some extent. Many low-level members are just silent, trying to live in this difficult time.

Would this come from members of the community?

This mainly comes from their political opponents. Another issue is the Jatiya Party (JP). They are not banned. However, whenever they try to organise activities, they face restrictions.

On freedom of expression, are people free to express their political views and are they free to protest?

We have concern over freedom of expression (FoE). Under the previous government, cases were filed under anti-terrorism (AT) law and the person was immediately put into jail. Initially, the IG allowed some space for FoE but gradually the IG also became a bit conservative about FoE, especially when a person was championing the rights of the opposition, they were accused of supporting the AL. Some journalists went to prison during the IG.

Now it is still a bit difficult to express opposition views, particularly if the view favours the AL in any way, so there are concerns about that, but the position until now has improved. Moving forward it will depend on the political strategy of the BNP regarding whether they allow the AL to carry out their regular activities or not. Until now, it appears that the BNP are running a ‘one-man show’ because they are not threatened by JeI and the NCP, so they can manage them and do not have that much interest in them. They cannot take challenge from a big opposition; they are enjoying this situation so they are not interested in allowing the AL to come back.

Was there any inter-/intra-party violence pre-election? What was the police response?

During the election period, violence was happening both inter- and intra-party. There was some violence within the BNP, and between the BNP and JeI, and we also saw some clashes with the NCP. So the clashes were multidimensional.

And in the post-election period?

Since the elections, instances of political violence have decreased and the situation has improved in some places, to some extent. Political violence is still going on, but mostly within the BNP, intra-party clashes and control over business interests, a system of extortion, who will take control of which area, what types of business will they control etc.

What has been the police response?

Some victims have tried to file cases against BNP activists, and the police have offered mediation, and then the perpetrator has escaped, so no case has been filed.

Post-election, has there been any state violence – if so, which security forces, ie at local or national level?

Most of the violence has been taking place at a local level.

Would you have an example of that?

Many journalists were arrested by the IG and many implicated in the July [2024] uprising and in the ICT cases, which is a big concern. Some other journalists were also arrested during the IG period for expressing opposition views that somehow do not favour the IG, or that may favour the AL’s view, though they were not necessarily supporting the AL. But they were expressing their view and put in jail. They got bail, but their cases are not withdrawn so they are awaiting trial.

On freedom of association, how is your organisation affected, are you able to operate freely?

Firstly, under the AL, we were under huge pressure as an organisation, there were directions that each and every proposal and suggestion should get approval from Sheikh Hasina’s office. Many proposals were delayed or blocked, and we were under surveillance. We were also under psychological pressure from law enforcement, so this made our work very difficult.

Under the IG, initially we saw that the situation was much improved. Our projects got approved quickly and funds were released. But gradually we saw the IG became very cautious about the activities of NGOs as well. For example, we applied for observation status for the National Elections (NE) with the Election Commission (EC), that was not granted. We had approval at some level but not by the EC on a technical issue. We tried to change this decision, however, we were told they did not have confidence we would support the government. So, after the election until now, the situation is comparatively better than under the AL government, but restrictions are not completely gone because we are seeing the old tactics of bureaucracy to frustrate, and the harassment of CSOs is coming back.

On the justice front, and regarding proposed reforms under the IG, have you seen any reform of the judiciary or any changes in the way that trials are processed?

Initially, there were some initiatives in the IG period, such as a separate secretariat for the Supreme Court, but the new government didn’t pass the ordinance in parliament, so this initiative is gone. The IG also made an ordinance on the Human Rights Commission (HRC), this was good and included many of our demands, but the new government also didn’t adopt it so we are back to an old 2009 law which is very restrictive and it actually sets a negative tone with the HRC. So some attempts of the IG for reform are actually gone.

Another thing about interfering with the judiciary during the IG period - on some occasions, some AL leaders and activists got bail. The law advisor was furious and said in public to go to the High Court and ask why they are granting bail to AL leaders and activists. There are still attempts to influence the position of the judiciary so it is not completely free.

What is the situation in relation to police independence now? Is there any government influence?

The police force usually try to figure out the sentiment of the government at the time, and if there is reward for loyalty then they will align with the government. They previously had complete loyalty to the AL government. There were hundreds and thousands of cases against AL activities. One view is that the police force were trying to flatter the [interim] government so they found some people and filed cases against these thousands of people, then they reported back to the top to say we have done these things; filed cases against AL leaders etc. Maybe this was another element that derailed the IG. That same thing is going on now, they can arrest some AL activists. The higher-ranking police officers, they publicly crack down, there is no change in the culture and practice.

Is it national or local – does it depend on the local influence of the police, or is it top down?

Many things go from down to up. What I was saying about the police forces who went to physically find false cases, this is a bottom-up idea. For example, this takes place in one or two places then the ‘high ups’ see this as an interesting thing that they are doing to help us, and say let us pick it up and make it policy, so then it comes from the top down.

For freedom of movement – if someone were to have a problem in one area could they move to another?

Yes, that is currently taking place, especially with AL cases. Leaders and activists facing cases in one district are trying to hide in another district or another area, and trying to pursue their business there. That is happening, they can move frequently, but it is a difficult situation.

Someone who is AL, can they express their opinion?

They can but it is difficult to express it publicly. When we are discussing with an AL activist, we may not like their ideas, but we are not attacking them. The problem is when they are saying things on social media or in electronic media, that is a problem. But at a community level, in day-to-day life, that is not a big problem. It is also true that sometimes people say we were doing good under Hasina’s regime, but when that belief is noticed in the public or in the media, then there is this case.

To clarify, organised activities would be different to political beliefs?

That is different. When 10 or 15 activists gather, use slogans, and place demands, that becomes difficult. But when they are separated and are talking (speaking privately) then that is not a big problem. A week after the election, many AL offices were reopened, but the BNP guys were trying to grab spaces and have some control.

One thing I want to add, India has become a big issue in Bangladesh at this moment, so we will see what happens. There are two types of conspiracy theories. One said that when Hasina loses control, she will take protection in India and that became true. The other is that Hasina said some political parties are trying to topple our government, and that also become true. We have seen that a large number of leaders/ activists have taken shelter in India, and that could not have been done overnight because they obtained property, have trade licenses etc, so India’s involvement in Bangladesh’s politics has become very negative.

Interview with Ayesha Kabir, Journalist

Date: 9 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Ayesha Kabir; 3 CPIT officials; 1 FCDO official

What is your role in your organisation and what is your current work focus?

I am a journalist. I work with the newspaper Prothom Alo, the leading newspaper in Bangladesh (although the information I am giving reflects my own opinions, rather than those of the organisation). I look after the English-language content of Prothom Alo and deal with everything on that side, but politics and security are my main interest and focus. I have worked at Prothom Alo for 12 years. Prothom Alo has a sound reputation, the reporting is objective, analytical and investigative. Over the past 2 decades, during the AL time, our ideology seemed almost identical to theirs: secularism, valuing the liberation war and democracy and human rights values.

We really suffered under the Awami League. They professed these ideals but in reality, it was a different story. We reported thoroughly on crime and corruption and came under a lot of repression and oppression from the government, the business community, those aligned with the (AL) government and from other sectors, even religious sectors. The AL claimed to be secular but would cater to some extreme religious groups. So, over those 15 years we went through a really bad time. Journalists were arrested, even one of our female crime journalists. Our editor, a very respected man, is now 80 years old but still very active. There were nearly 60 cases against him all over the country.

There was just sheer harassment. For example, in terms of low levels of oppression, say this meeting today, I wouldn’t have agreed to it, as if I left the office I would have been followed and then faced questioning. Journalists faced both subtle and deep harassment during the Awami League time.

We were active during the fall of the Awami League. Many photojournalists and journalists were injured. During the interim government, to tell the truth, I felt a huge sense of relief. We have not let up our ideology, or our goal to always report on crime, corruption, irregularities, but there was sense of relief that we were managing to do that.

However, during the interim government, many had doubts about their intention after 15 years of the whole system being politicised. It wasn’t easy for a non-political government. The police force was shattered, there was corruption in the bureaucracy and in every institution, so it was difficult to run the country. During this time, we came under attack. There was the sprouting of mobs under the guise of religious elements. We don’t know absolutely for certain who was behind them but it would be good to know. Our building was burnt down, they smashed everything including valuable equipment, luckily there weren’t many journalists in the building and they were all safe. The mobs burnt down everything. It was really traumatic, financially too. They also attacked the [Bangladesh] Daily Star. During the interim government, there were other incidents of mob violence on a smaller scale.

Then, this government came to power. So far, I’m not saying it has been perfect but that sense of relief has been revived. We have been reporting again about certain weaknesses, the government is not perfect in many ways but we haven’t come under attack for our reporting. We are able to do it freely, with no repercussions. This is talking about us [as journalists]. That is it in a nutshell.

The mobs under the interim government who were responsible for violence, was there accountability? Was justice pursued?

We were very upset on two accounts. No law enforcement came forward to prevent this. We had got warning when the crowd naturally gathered at a distance beforehand. We reported this to the Home Ministry and police. Police only arrived very late and so did the fire engines. The fire engines were prevented from coming close. It was only after the damage had been done that the police actually came to the scene. People have been arrested but they were people who didn’t orchestrate it. The interim government had turned a blind eye to this. There are certain elements outside the country who use social media to incite violence. They incite religious elements, but they are not necessarily religious. There’s one man who is stationed in France, he’s a well-known Hindu man, but he incited the Islamic community by saying Prothom Alo is atheist. The incident was very traumatic. Everyone in the interim government was apologetic after the damage was done.

The cases are ongoing; there have been more people arrested but the actual matter hasn’t been totally solved.

Around election time, did your organisation receive hostility around election reporting?

Not really. We didn’t have any issues, and the election went quite smoothly. There were warnings and threats, but we could report on the election, even on any irregularities that may have occurred in the election.

Regarding the harassment you talked about, are there any legal restrictions now on your activities that prevent freedom of speech?

Officially we haven’t got any warnings.

The Prime Minister has been interacting with media houses and editors occasionally. We haven’t been threatened yet. I don’t know how long it will last as it is still quite early for the new administration. We are sceptical of how far it can change. But so far, the vibe has been good.

The Prime Minister has been very positive. The speeches he has done, everyone appreciates, even people who are politically neutral. Since he has come to power, he hasn’t been abusive towards the previous government under Sheikh Hasina. She would use filthy language against him, terrible language, and would say things against our paper and editor. It was very crude. In that sense, there has been no vengeance from the new Prime Minister. It is a good thing. Some of his ministers sometimes say things they shouldn’t.

But the problem lies at the grassroots level. Everything is politicised. The AL were in power in towns and districts, running businesses and extortion schemes. The BNP have that sentiment that “it is our turn now” in these local areas. The government/central power have a difficult time controlling those at the grassroots. For example, my office is in the middle of a market, previously it was the AL or their student league who would collect tolls from shopkeepers and rickshaw drivers, now it’s the BNP men (though to a lesser extent). In the bigger cities, they [central leadership/government] are managing to control it to an extent but at the grassroots it is more difficult to control. It’s not that the government aren’t trying to control this, but it’s not always possible. It’s a big drawback, but we will see how far they go in controlling this.

The ministers, there are a lot of new faces, that is a good thing. But the newly appointed Bangladesh governor, the central bank governor, is a businessman, that is a huge conflict. This came as a surprise and a disappointment. I am not saying that he’s incompetent, but it’s a conflict of interests.

Under the new government, has there been any more discussion about how they proceed with the reform commissions put forward under the interim government? Has there been any progress?

They have been very slow at that. When the reforms were being formulated, BNP had a lot of points they disagreed with and they did note their dissent. They have been a bit slow on reform and that is where the opposition is objecting. The BNP are saying that they will carry out reforms slowly.

It can sometimes be one step forward and two steps back. They have brought in certain positive things from their own manifestos. Under the previous government, ministers and MPs would get duty free cars cheap and that has now stopped. They also used to get huge plots of land for hardly any money but that has stopped. Lots of things like that have been stopped.

[This information was added after the meeting The previous prime minister(s) had a lot of protocol that would cause public inconvenience. A huge entourage of cars accompanying them wherever they went. Roads being blocked for long periods of time when the Prime Minister was to pass. Huge accommodation and extravagant perks. The present Prime Minister is more down to earth in this regard. No fanfare of toadeaters [hangers on] following him around.]

No reforms of the anti-corruption and information commission have been done yet. Nothing has been done about these institutions. I personally feel reforms are needed in the civil service. There has been a lot of corruption and politicisation in the civil service and police. The government is professing that they are reforming these, and they are making small steps, but they are not doing enough. In the judiciary and civil service, they are ostensibly removing one set of partisan people for another set of partisan people. Perhaps not as extreme as in the past, but the remains the case.

How does the local influence of the AL play into the actions of the police at that level? Previously and now?

Just as the BNP was a popular party, the AL was huge party and a popular party. They were an old party who were involved in the liberation war and ostensibly led liberation. They claim that they freed the country (even though everyone was involved). They always had to have the upper hand and some of those people are still there.

In the election, a lot of people sided with the BNP or even JeI, so they are still there, they are still active. The police, if they wanted to, could have done a lot with the grassroots but they are still corrupt, they might be working on behalf of the AL, or the BNP, so that is there and we must not forget that the AL have got huge amounts of money and they are using that to keep up the corruption. We shouldn’t blame them alone, but we can’t rule that out. It’s all well being the good cop and putting on a nice face, but when it comes to the people’s sake, I think the government needs to be much, much stricter.

Do you think government has control over security forces and is there a BNP directive of how police should act at lower levels?

I must bring in JeI as a factor too because until the IG came into power, because they were opposed to the formation of the 1971 war with Pakistan, they had a black label and negative image, but when the AL needed them they would use them to fight against the BNP. They have never had many seats in parliament; they have had very few. When the IG came, not only is JeI a very religious party, they got the upper hand, because the ban against them was lifted and the interim government gave them a lot of leeway. Other religious groups managed to also raise their heads.

What was disappointing was that the young people who had led the July/August [2024] movement, the young people on the streets, who managed to put a fight against Sheikh Hasina. These young people managed to do it even though the major political opposition had struggled to oust Hasina. They had such a large following during July/August [2024], parents and grandparents were even joining them on the streets or taking food for them, there was a lot of hope put into these young people.

It is disappointing because many of these young people are now regressive instead of progressive.

People would ask, are they [young people] disillusioned that the BNP came into power. But these young people and the NCP were part of that anti-government movement, they were really strong. They should have remained so, instead of themselves becoming like political forces which they opposed.

Many of them are regressive. We imagined them to be progressive. You can be religious and progressive but they became regressive, anti-LGBT, and not anti-women but against women’s progress and women’s participation in sport, trying to dictate how women should dress in public, etc. This is what started and the young people initiated it, and we were disappointed with Professor Yunus being in power. He didn’t do anything to stop this trend. Many of the young people who were in the movement were pretty happy when our office was attacked. When the election came, the NCP imagined a sweeping victory but people didn’t vote for them. They got seats but when they realised they wouldn’t get that many seats, they joined with JeI and they managed to get enough seats. [This information was added after the meeting They should have been more realistic and not expected to sweep to power in the very first election that was held. After all, they were new to politics and inexperienced. They were popular, but they needed to be patient and build up public confidence in them.]

And also, about the AL itself, the AL government would speak harshly about BNP activities, leaders, and PM Tarique himself. He was mistreated and oppressed by the AL, you would imagine there would be a blood bath of revenge (AL professed it would be so). His [Tarique Rahman’s] mother was an uncompromising leader, she could have left the country if she chose to, she was really mistreated, as was Tarique himself too. But there hasn’t been that backlash, or vengeance at all, even at the grassroots. At the beginning, yes, certain symbols and Hasina’s father’s house was burnt down, this is during the IG, so all of this happened then, but now also there hasn’t been any backlash.

The AL was a dynastic party; Sheikh Hasina or her family were the leaders, other than them nobody has been at the head. Even now, she [Hasina] refuses to let go, she is in India. The AL is a bit of a cult rather than a party so the party also say ‘Hasina or nobody’, they are not letting go. There are many people who would like to come forward, it is such an old, traditional party, with such a lot of support, but they have no regret, remorse, or admitting that they made mistakes. When we lived through times of enforced disappearances, keeping people detained in small and cramped rooms for months or years at a time, it was scary, like in medieval times.

Are there any reports of enforced disappearances?

No, there are no enforced disappearances now. Just arrests

Has there been any accountability for lower-level AL people accused of human rights abuses, those that are still in Bangladesh?

That’s a big thing about the politicians and others, including journalists, jailed during the interim government, a lot of them are still in jail. Some have been released and some cases are still going on. There has been a lot of talk on this.

There are two opinions on these cases. One is that maybe they were guilty. Some journalists were known to have aided and abetted Sheikh Hasina by saying enforced disappearances didn’t happen and such. Journalists are usually overworked and underpaid, but some of these people became like millionaires overnight, driving big cars etc. Maybe they deserve to be arrested for this but the cases against them are flimsy. They deserve to be punished for crimes, but they can’t be kept in jail with these flimsy cases. I tell those in the legal field ‘why don’t you fight to get evidence?’ or get journalists to come forward with evidence. Then fresh cases can be filed against them. But like it or not, keeping them behind bars with no evidence is wrong.

Recently, many of them have been released. We recently had a huge media conference within Bangladesh, alongside politicians from other countries. Some of these journalists who have been released were invited but they came with no remorse. They had the same sense of entitlement and asked why they aren’t getting jobs. There’s no sense of remorse or regret about how corrupt they have been. Justice and law is not one and the same, unfortunately.

According to the law, I know that some of them should be released or maybe just questioned. At the same time, there are some who have been released who maybe shouldn’t have been. There are corrupt. Business people not in the country now that are looking at maybe returning. At the same time, the government has been trying to get back the laundered money. To me, corruption is one of the main problems in our country and these people have so much money that it’s easy to buy their way out.

Those who were held on politically-motivated charges during the protests, many have been released. Are you aware of any that have not been released, for example students?

Most of them have been released, I’m not aware of any cases where they have not been.

This is a legal question. If a politically-motivated arrest warrant was issued under the AL, would that still be legally valid?

It would still stand because of the code of criminal procedure. So as far as I know it would still stand.

Do you know whether there would be a direction issued on how to deal with those cases and whether those warrants would be enforced?

I couldn’t give an exact or accurate answer to that.

Are you aware of any official statistics on arrests and detentions of people over the years?

Not off the top of my head.

And the same question about violence, any official statistics?

Again, not off the top of my head.

You have touched upon police efficacy; if someone in the local community, in say JeI, had problems in the community, would they be able to seek protection from the police?

Yes they would be. I wouldn’t call the police inefficient. But they don’t have enough capacity even if they want to help, because many of them fled after the AL was ousted from power.

Jel have ‘infiltrated’ themselves into the police, military, armed forces, in different areas of bureaucracy, especially during the interim government. Even beforehand, Jel have a very different format than the BNP and AL. They are like a communist party, very regimented, very dedicated. The AL has a student wing and Jel infiltrated there, committing crimes in the name of the student party, but the moment the IG came in they said they were Jel students. They are very efficient like that.

If you look at the BNP or AL, the AL is like a cult and the BNP is like a club. Jel are extremely regimented and dedicated. In the AL, other than Sheikh Hasina, you can’t think who would be the next leader. The BNP has an element of dynasties, Tarique [Rahman]’s father was president (although the BNP would not be fanatical like AL). Whereas Jel is just like a communist party, the present head of JeI, we hadn’t heard much of him before. He’s got a relatively more modern outlook. He [the Jel leader] was shunned before, but the moment the AL fell, now when he goes to events at foreign embassies, the diplomats rush to meet Jel. There were suddenly accepted into society, which they didn’t have before.

Regarding a person’s political leanings, does that affect whether they can get police protection in their community, generally?

It has been like that so far. Since the changeover, a bit less than before [under the AL]. Naturally, that is there, but before, the AL was all-encompassing, but right now it’s a mixed bag so it’s not that bad, but the corruption is still there in the police.

You touched on student wings, what’s their role in political parties?

They are the muscle men for the political parties, and it’s always been like that. Before, they were very politicised but it was seen very positively. I lived through 1971, they were leading in the movement for the Liberation War, then the military leader was in power, they were leading in the movement for his downfall, and always seemed very positive. I was in university, even though the BNP was in power, it was the left-wing student league who were very powerful.

The student wings weren’t hoodlums or extortionists, but things slowly changed and they became corrupt. For example, contracts for repairing buildings were given to student leaders and they would make so much money. If you were part of a student group, only that group would be able to stay in the halls, so it was complete exploitation. Student halls have gone completely, that has been removed now – they were like torture chambers their halls, they would make 50 people stay in a small room until you pledged your loyalty to them, that has gone now.

How closely aligned are they with the policies of their main party?

Because the policies of the main parties are just actually theory, and previously it was the AL ruling the country and making money, ideologically there was a lot of things they couldn’t say. It was blasphemy to speak against the AL or Sheikh Hasina.

Right now, it’s almost like people are waiting for the other shoe to drop. Everything has been going well, but it is not perfect, with the police and judiciary a lot of reforms are needed. [PM] Tarique is giving out good vibes, but how far can the BNP keep it up? The government, policy-wise, is good. People want to believe in them, but once bitten, twice shy.

Social media is a big factor too, it’s full of disinformation. People read our newspaper because it is so reliable, so we are constantly having to point out this and that is fake etc. People like to be believe what’s not true, so that’s a constant battle that the government is having to deal with too, but how effective they are we’ll see, it’s still early days. But, PM Tarique, I think he is fine. The ministers, so far, so good, but we are so used to seeing corruption, it is hard not to be cynical.

Interview with Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem (also known as Barrister Arman) Jamaat e Islami MP for Dhaka-14

Date: 8 June 2026

Location: Bangladesh Parliament Building, Dhaka

Present: Mir Ahmad Bin Quasem (also known as Barrister Arman), Jamaat e Islami MP; 3 CPIT officials; 2 FCDO officials

Could you outline your role within your political party and your current aims and objectives?

I first have to talk about the past. I was a victim of enforced disappearance and was held incommunicado in Aynaghar for 8 years. It’s important to explain this because it shapes what we are doing now. I was released after the revolution [July/August 2024]. No-one thought they would see me again, except my wife and mother who never gave up hope. Because of this, I know first-hand what it’s like to be a political dissident and be under a government with unchecked power.

I am a practising Barrister at the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. My Head of Chambers, Barrister A Raazzaq, has said our constitution gives power to the head of state similar to a Roman emperor. We want balance of power, accountability and transparency.

The current legal regime consolidates power in too few hands. [To change this] we need to implement the July Charter. It would bring real accountability, and it is something we want to see through. I am Member of Parliament for Mirpur in the east end of Dhaka. It is one of the poorest and most neglected parts of the city. I was born and raised there. Most people assume Mirpur is full of elites and wealth, but they are wrong. In reality, there are people living in poverty and they live in worse conditions than in many rural areas. The reason they elected me is because I called for real change and an overhaul of the system. People are not happy with the current system.

As well as being an MP, I am also the Advisor of Foreign Affairs to the Leader of the Opposition. In this role, I engage with stakeholders such as international politicians, communities and press. I am assigned to liaise with the outside world on behalf of the party.

Our main goal is to overhaul the system. We are not happy with the constitution and penal system, unless implementation of significant change is brought in compliance with the July Charter as promised during the election. Right now, the judiciary, the anti-corruption commission, and the civil bureaucracy provide almost no real check on the executive. Put simply, our institutions are not working as they should.

How has the political environment changed since August 2024, including under the interim government and now?

First, we have leadership who held public office before back in office. Our country has never had a strong record on accountability or tolerating dissent, and unfortunately the new government has not been different so far. Usually, we do not get to see many new faces in government, but it is different in this parliament as 2 thirds of MPs are new. Even so, “the old guard” mentality is in control, so little has changed. Principles and policies have taken a back seat, and we are back to the old way of doing business. It is how we saw things in past; policy pushed through by force. Policy is driven little by concept, it is done by the ruling class and individuals with business interests to see how much they can gain. It is more transactional.

During the interim government, we saw signs of real reform, and they had a clear plan to see this out. We are now seeing that vanishing and big decisions are being based on “transactions”. I am happy to say that on record.

What is your party’s relationship with the BNP now?

The BNP is our brother in arms; we have been in alliance for over 21 years, and we were part of the government together. Back then, our interests were mutual and we shared a common adversary. During the election period, we fought the election against each other and now one of us is in government and the other in opposition, but we still have a working relationship.

We see the government is trying to portray tolerance in parliament when getting criticism from political leadership. We don’t see a political backlash just because we have criticised them. There is a semblance of tolerance there but there are signs of that moving away. For example, 7 online activists have been detained so far for criticising government officials or the work of the government. We are only 100 days in and there have been 7 arrests merely because they were critical of the government. As tensions grow and the government makes more politically driven decisions, we expect to criticise more, which increases the risk. In general, power and tolerance move in opposite directions: the more power is concentrated, the less tolerant those in power tend to become. People fear that as power consolidates further, legal reform will stall.

You’ve touched on tolerance at a higher level – what about the tolerance at constituency or grassroots level – what is the BNP’s tolerance for Jamaat in the community?

Dhaka is different [from the rest of the country]. In other areas, government policies are fuelling divide. For example, when distributing government grants for members of parliament, it is meant to be equal. They are deliberately leaving MPs out of grants. Government grants are being given to ruling party people, even in areas where the MP is part of the opposition. I’ll share the brief we have prepared on systematic exclusion. They leave the opposition out of grants, which is giving rise to tensions on the ground.

Dhaka is a bit different, there is law and order and police presence to stop it getting out of hand and becoming a bigger issue. In rural areas, there is only about one policeman for every 7,000 people and there have been a few demonstrations where dissenting opinion has converted into commotion. We have already seen a dozen serious injuries and at least one death linked to police confrontations.

Is that pre-election?

No, this has continued even after the election. In the Bangladesh context, one death is not abnormal. I am not proud to say that, but one or two deaths doesn’t make headlines. When a fellow student died, we staged a demonstration; people were surprised there was a demonstration over one person who died. That’s the reality, that it hardly makes headlines. That shows how normalised this has become. My concern is that this could get worse as political tension increases.

Around freedom of expression, you’ve mentioned protesting - what is the situation now? Can your members protest and how does that compare to the period under Awami League rule?

Under the Awami League (AL), repression was institutionalised under the oppressive Cyber Security Act which criminalised social media posts criticising the government. There is now a new law proposed, aimed at misinformation and deliberate posts targeting racial and communal tensions. They are trying to bring back the old law in a new name, and their statement is that it is to counter misinformation. If provision is reinstated, it might be abused. They are not saying it’s against political dissidents and political criticism isn’t in the scope of the law, but the law isn’t rigorous. If the new law goes through, everyone deciding to criticise the government might face criminal prosecution under the new law. We don’t believe in this law, there is scope for prosecution based on fabrications and trumped-up charges.

In developing countries, the police and judiciary can be used as a political tool against the opposition, and we have seen this happen before in Bangladesh. At the moment, it is not widescale, but without reform and major amendments to branches of power, there is nothing preventing this.

Were there protests around the election and post-election period and what was the police response?

It was a very peaceful election, we didn’t see any major violence. Even after the result, many were not happy as they believed people’s views were not reflected. We decided to accept the result for the sake of the stability of the country. Because of this more patient stance from the opposition, we haven’t seen much post-election violence.

However, there was violence around two recent by-elections. In Sherpur, one person died, and we saw serious problems – armed groups took control of polling stations, among other issues.

[This information was added after the meeting Several senior leaders from the ruling party contested multiple seats in the general election. After winning, they retained one seat each, triggering by-elections for the vacated seats.]

Which groups were involved?

This was the BNP against Jamaat e Islami. There was violence, and the physical expulsion of polling officers. Polling centres were occupied by ruling party-linked groups and they won the by-election.

What was the police response?

They [the police] were bystanders and watched from afar, they simply did not act. The military were deployed during the general election and were more proactive in stopping problems and ensuring fair votes. In my area, out of 177 polls at least 30 were taken over by such groups during the general election, and the military was quick to expel these thugs; we didn’t see the military taking any actions against miscreants in the by-elections.

On justice and accountability, is there any update on those held for their actions under Sheikh Hasina? There has been media attention on the ICT charges of high-profile people, but has there been anything in relation to lower profile people or action in the normal domestic courts?

To be very honest, those who could afford a good lawyer and were not charged under the ICT, the majority of them have been released. After the BNP came to power, there were a significant amount of people linked with the Awami League who were granted bail. The assumption is that they somehow ended up manging to have a “back channel” with the ruling party.

In my area, local leaders who fired automatic weapons at protesters are now out on bail, which was a shock to us. Those who could afford a good lawyer or had the capacity to get a back channel with the ruling party are now out. That didn’t happen with the ICT, as at that higher level there are more checks and balances, and the cases have lots of attention.

In the rural areas, a significant number of cases have been bailed. The former speaker of Awami League was released within 3 weeks, and 2 MPs who were jailed during the interim period are out. From what we hear from within the legal community, including a friend who is defending AL members, they are very optimistic they will get out on bail. The political urge that they don’t get bail is not there anymore. In short, those who can get a back channel into government [have the right connections] and those who can get a good lawyer can get out.

What about the independence of the judiciary and the judicial system?

As a lawyer, I used to pride myself as an officer of the court but with the way things are now, I’m not proud. During the interim government, an independent judicial secretariat was set up but has now been dissolved. The ruling party promised to bring it back in a stronger form, but we are still waiting for that. Once in power, any executive is tempted to control everything, including the judiciary – and that is what has happened here; this reform has not moved forward.

Proposed laws from the interim government had to be approved by the full parliament and many of these have been allowed to lapse. The judicial community and human rights groups have been pushing for the reinstating of the law. The government have been saying they will bring it back in a “year or two” but based on what we are seeing, we doubt this will actually happen – which speaks volumes on the intentions of the ruling party.

Is there an update on those held on politically motivated charges under Hasina? Do people remain in custody and if so on what charges, and what is the profile of such people?

Most people held on politically motivated charges under Sheikh Hasina’s government, including those with a political background, have been released. However, some people accused of crimes during the 1971 Liberation War are still in prison. The fate of these cases hasn’t changed much. Also, those held for the border guard mutiny during the AL, 175 have been executed so far, and those who were not executed but serving a life sentence are still inside.

Is it a unique profile of cases?

Yes.

If an arrest warrant was issued against a political opponent and was not executed during that period, does it still stand legally now? What is the process of a warrant being executed?

Legally, there is no time limit on the validity of a warrant, unless there is a revision by law or it is taken back by the relevant police department. If there no action taken to withdraw the warrant, then it remains valid indefinitely. That is the legal position.

But, in practice, the police are understaffed, overburdened and underfunded. Even a valid warrant may never really be enforced.

So, in practice, say a Jamaat supporter previously had an arrest warrant, would that be pursued?

I know of 2 Jamaat leaders who, due to a fear of prosecution, fled during the AL rule and when they returned, they were detained at the airport. They were taken to court and released on bail. One warrant was in place for 7 years and now that there is a digital system, a warrant will remain there forever and you can get caught no matter how many years later. Those with existing warrants may get arrested on return, they may get bail or may be detained for a few days, or after a long time, it depends on the degree of severity of the charges.

Does it go through the court process?

Yes, it has to go through the legal process and then they get bail. One of the senior religious leaders accused by the AL had to go through the legal process to get out. He spent time in jail but then got out and the case was closed.

And the people who took part in the 2024 protests, students etc who were initially arrested, do any remain detained?

No – all of them have been released.

But there are growing concerns about “July protesters”. In the media and especially on talk shows from AL supporters, journalists and those with international backgrounds are questioning whether they should be detained for the killing of police officers. Some of the “July warriors” are expressing concerns that AL leaders getting bail might mean they retaliate and that the BNP are not owning up to their part in the July [2024] revolution. Those who were the most visible are finding themselves without support, they are worried about safety and security.

Those affiliated with the Awami League who remain in the community, do they still have power and influence?

Those in the AL had a long tenure in power and gained a significant amount of wealth and business. The BNP has resorted to the transactional approach to governing and are able to extract benefits from them because of this.

I wouldn’t be surprised that an AL leader with financial capacity might go after prominent local participants in the July [2024] movement for vindication. I wouldn’t be surprised if this happened, even based on business disputes. When the AL were in power, those with business disputes couldn’t go anywhere for protection. During the interim government, members of the local community generally had the upper hand in land and business disputes, but now that AL figures are back out on bail, they are trying to reclaim that position, often bypassing the courts entirely. This is a genuine concern.

On police capacity to deal with issues at the local level – would someone be able to go to the police with a political problem and would it depend on which political party was involved?

Honestly, it depends on the capacity of the victim. If the victim has the capacity to draw attention in practical means, i.e. through social media or financially, they might get relief. And the other factor is the attention given to the case by the ruling party, if they get involved nothing will help the victim.

In my constituency, one of my key campaign promises was to tackle corruption and extortion. In the downtown area, gangs were running an extortion racket. One of my campaign promises was to make sure this doesn’t happen as they were terrorising local businesses. I asked someone to help organise local businessmen against this – and he was subsequently charged by ruling party-linked individuals with intimidating local businesses. He was just trying to gather businessmen against extortion and now he’s being charged with intimidation. The only reason for this is that the gang have an informal alliance with the BNP-linked figures who take a cut of the proceeds. I called the police commissioner, and he couldn’t help because he couldn’t get back to the area and he has a warrant in his name. I’m an MP and I’m calling the police saying that this man is innocent, he did it on my instruction to gather businessmen. They said they are powerless and advised talking to local ruling party leaders in my area. The police force does not have a history of independence, and that has not changed.

I hope that someone will read this and do something to change it. We have to admit that something is broken and to change it. Trying to sugar coat it won’t change it. This is the situation, the first step to fixing it is to admit it is broken.

Around the role of auxiliary groups, particularly student wings – can you explain how it works and their links to the main party?

The BNP, AL and Jamaat all have student wings. The BNP and AL have a similar modus, they are two sides of same coin when it comes to their political structures.

Jamaat is different: we are more internally democratic and disciplined. Our student wing, Shibir, has no official organisational link to Jamaat. They are an independent organisation, even Jamaat cannot dictate who will be president. When it comes to the BNP, their constitution gives its party chair the power to appoint the head of its student wing, making it formally part of the party structure. Ours is different and independent. We don’t have organisational control over the student wing. In practice, when there are common issues or goals, they join us together, for example at the moment we are protesting on freedom of speech so we may join together in protest.

The BNP and AL’s constitutions specify that the head of the student wing will be decided by the party leader. In terms of the student wing organisation, it is part and parcel of the wider party machine, in both law and practice. In our constitution they are totally separate, Shibir is completely independent in practice.

Jamaat leaders allow its students to have a mind of their own. They are local observers, they can verify more, they are more politically agile and more locally connected. During the interim government, they won Student Union elections in public universities, but we couldn’t replicate that in the general election. Shibir are more adaptive to change, the main organisation is not that flexible. Jamaat has an internal council through which the Ameer [leader] and other leaders are elected by party members and this council does not happen in other parties.

The AL, unlike the BNP, has not changed its organisational practices in over 15 years, in either its main party or its student wings. In both the BNP and AL, the leaders of the student wings tend to be older, they rarely change the leader, and they are effectively chosen by the party leadership – even positions like the vice-president of the student wing.

No clear distinction emerged during the discussion. Examples discussed, such as late notification of court appearances, appeared to reflect concerns that had also been reported more generally in relation to the functioning of the justice system. The discussion also referred to observations reportedly shared by organizations with longstanding engagement on detention-related issues in Bangladesh.

A number of stakeholders, including the ICRC [International Committee of the Red Cross] and the EU reportedly noted that many of the described detention-related concerns or proceeding-related shortcomings appeared consistent with longstanding structural challenges affecting the judiciary and detention conditions more broadly. From an analytical perspective, it was observed that establishing differentiated treatment would require a much more detailed factual assessment. The discussion highlighted that distinguishing between systemic shortcomings and treatment linked specifically to political affiliation would require detailed case-by-case analysis.

From a human rights professional perspective, such distinctions are often found in the practical implementation of detention regimes rather than in the formal rules themselves, and therefore require detailed, facility-specific and case-by-case assessment. For example, where a general practice permits contact with the outside world at regular intervals, differentiated treatment may instead be reflected in subtle variations in how that practice is applied to particular individuals. Similarly, access to medical care may appear comparable in principle while differing in practice through delays or more restrictive application affecting particular detainees. These are often highly fact-specific issues that can only be identified through detailed and sustained case-by-case monitoring. The arguments of the EU and the ICRC are totally relevant, and it needs assessing in more detail to get a sense on if there is discrimination grounded on political affiliation.

From a comparative human rights perspective, political transitions often require close observation of institutional practices over time. It is often these subtle differences in practice that require sustained observation in order to determine whether differentiated treatment exists. In other contexts with comprehensive monitoring mandates, including through regular engagement with places of detention, it was possible to develop a much more detailed understanding of institutional practices over time. The current operational framework in Bangladesh is different and therefore does not provide the same basis for such assessments.]
