Interview with Mosifiqur Rahman Johan, Chairman of All Victims and Veteran Network

Date: 14 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Mosifiqur Rahman Johan, Chairman of All Victims and Veteran Network (AVN); 3 CPIT officials

Introduction

I’m a human rights activist, and work in a multi-disciplinary way, engaging with different organisations to have maximum impact. For 7/8 years I worked with an organisation called Maayer Daak that was a platform for victims and their families of enforced disappearance. We carried out demonstrations. I also work for AVN - All Victims and Veteran network in Bangladesh, of enforced disappearances and extra judicial killings, we connect with victims. At the moment, I am trying to organise some protests on human rights.

Broadly, how has the political environment changed since August 2024?

There have been so many frustrations. During the [protest] movement, our understanding was that the political system would change and so many institutions would change, for example the police, civil, and judicial institutions. We believed they were not functioning, but we were not sure how we moved forward from this space, this was the struggle. Since the uprising, many people from different sectors came but there were broken promises in a way. It has been extremely difficult to navigate in that direction, and the Interim Government (IG) made so many commissions which is really good, but the problem is they didn’t know how to implement them. So, they don’t add any value because they were not implemented. Also, the Human Rights Commission and the Enforced Disappearance ordinance, all of them have lapsed. So, our comment is that we have to ensure that we build new institutions and new policies, so that we will build a new Bangladesh.

The current situation remains confrontational, the mass people [the masses] are not happy. The BNP is in government now, but they are struggling because it is a deep-rooted problem, it is rooted in infrastructure. The BNP now has to take control of the police and civil administration.

Also, the political opposition sometimes don’t have that legitimacy, so it is quite complicated to push and quite complicated to see how all of the parties are navigating these dimensions.

With the changes in the political environment, has that affected different political groups?

The political landscape has certainly changed, and so have the roles of many political actors. Groups such as the BNP and Jamaat, which were previously victims of repression under the Awami League government, now hold considerably more political influence. However, I do not think they have consistently upheld the standards they once demanded from those in power.

The situation today is not as severe as it was under the previous regime, but that does not mean the underlying problems have disappeared. One of the biggest disappointments has been the lack of commitment to meaningful reform. After the uprising, many of us hoped that the kinds of human rights violations we witnessed during the Awami League era - such as arbitrary arrests, politically motivated cases, and abuses of state power - would not be repeated.

[This information was added after the meeting Instead, while the scale may be different, some of the same patterns continue to emerge. That raises concerns about whether there has been a genuine shift in political culture or simply a change in who holds power. The real test of democratic transition is not only replacing those in government, but ensuring that the institutions and practices that enabled abuse are fundamentally reformed.]

Has the newly elected BNP government implemented any recommendations from the commissions formed under the interim government – if so, what?

They gave up on the idea of implementing the recommendations but said that they will implement new laws that would be modified by them. Regarding the Human Rights Commission ordinance, who will be the law enforcement agency? It should be an independent body, not the institution themselves. Now it’s complex, if the police, for example, have committed extra-judicial killings or custodial torture, who will do the investigation? They (the BNP) are saying they came up with a new law and it has to be changed, the institution (i.e. the police) will essentially investigate themselves.

In terms of members and leaders of political organisations, are they able to freely express their political opinions?

At the moment, people are generally able to express their political opinions more freely than they could under the previous government. The situation is better, although I am not sure that this openness will necessarily last.

One of the biggest challenges is that society is deeply traumatised. Many people have experienced arbitrary arrests, torture, enforced disappearances, or other forms of repression. These experiences have left lasting psychological and social scars. At the same time, there is still no strong human rights protection mechanism or comprehensive process for truth, accountability, and justice. Many victims continue to struggle to obtain justice or even official recognition of what happened to them.

Because of this, it is difficult for society to move forward. If we want to build a new Bangladesh, we need a shared understanding of the past and a credible process for accountability that is based on the rule of law rather than revenge. One of the most difficult questions concerns how to navigate the Awami League period. I do not think there is yet a clear or widely accepted approach to that issue.

These are questions that Bangladesh will have to confront in the coming years. If they remain unresolved, there is a real risk that the country will fall back into another cycle of political violence and retaliation instead of breaking with the past.

Is there any update on those held for their actions under the Hasina regime? Are people still in custody? On what charges? At what stage of the process, i.e. proceeding towards trial?

There are currently two main legal tracks for addressing crimes committed during the Hasina government: the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) and the ordinary criminal courts.

[This information was added after the meeting From what I have observed, the ICT process is moving in a relatively structured direction, following its legal procedures. However, the ordinary courts present a more complicated picture. A large number of Awami League members and supporters have been charged, and there are concerns that some individuals who were not personally responsible for serious crimes have also become defendants. That raises important questions about individual criminal responsibility and due process.

The ICT itself also has a complicated legacy. Historically, it has been criticised for its use of the death penalty and other due process concerns. While it is now dealing with a different set of crimes, those institutional legacies remain relevant. At the same time, the tribunal is working under significant time and political pressure to investigate an enormous number of cases.

I work closely with many victims and families who have filed complaints with the ICT. One of their biggest frustrations is the lack of information about the progress of investigations, particularly in cases involving people who remain disappeared and have never returned. Families often do not know what evidence has been collected, whether investigations are progressing, or who may ultimately be held accountable.

Another major challenge is that enforced disappearances and other state crimes were carried out through institutional structures rather than by a single individual. A victim might be abducted by one law enforcement agency, transferred to another unit, detained in secret facilities, and processed through multiple layers of officials. Responsibility was often distributed across different institutions and chains of command. Because of that, identifying only a handful of direct perpetrators cannot fully explain how the system operated or ensure comprehensive accountability.

As the ICT continues its investigations, some suspects are likely to be arrested, while others have already left the country or may evade prosecution. But the larger challenge is uncovering the institutional system that enabled these crimes. Without addressing those structural issues - not only prosecuting a limited number of individuals - it will be difficult to achieve meaningful transitional justice and prevent similar abuses from happening again.]

And how about the lower levels, who are the people going through the normal courts?

[This information was added after the meeting In the ordinary courts, there have been many cases against Awami League members and supporters. Some have been subject to arbitrary arrest, while others have later been released. At the same time, there are concerns that some of those most responsible for serious human rights violations have not yet been held accountable. That distinction is important.

The central challenge is identifying and prosecuting those who bear the greatest responsibility for these crimes, rather than pursuing broad or politically motivated cases. Accountability should be based on credible evidence and individual responsibility.

The Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances has released material that illustrates the complexity of these cases. In one public interview, a retired senior military officer, Lieutenant General Akbar, described how enforced disappearances were carried out and stated that he had raised concerns directly with Sheikh Hasina, who reportedly said she would look into the matter. After making those statements, he left Bangladesh and is now reported to be in India.

Cases like this raise important questions. If individuals who may have crucial information about how the system operated are able to leave the country without being questioned or brought before investigators, it inevitably affects public confidence in the accountability process.

There have been arrests of some political figures, but many victims continue to ask whether those who designed, authorised, or coordinated the system of enforced disappearances and other serious abuses are actually being held accountable. Without a genuine commitment to identifying the principal perpetrators and ensuring fair, evidence-based prosecutions, it will be difficult to build public trust in the justice process.]

For those who were arrested for politically motivated charges under the Hasina government, reporting indicates some have been released. Are there any still imprisoned, and if so, what is their profile?

Have you heard of knee-capping? Knee-capping under the AL was when the police took a person then they tortured them. When they were in the police custody at night, police took them to a silent place, mostly in areas by the river or the forest, and they shot them in the knees. Later they would file charges against them and say it happened in a gunfight. They would go to prison. There are around 185 cases like this. I have interviewed 35 people in this situation, I try to do analytical research. As I said, they are the victims in that they have lost their whole legs, but since the police filed the case against them, some of them are in prison. Now even after 10-15 years, many cases are not resolved yet. Last week I saw two people in custody who were the victims of the last regime. They [the victims] were BNP and Jamaat e Islami, they were opposition. You have to resolve the case, the interim government didn’t come up with a brilliant idea. Also, the BNP, those are the victims, now some of the leaders from the BNP told the victims to resolve these kinds of cases, that is the problem.

Regarding arrest warrants under the Hasina government, against the opposition, would those arrest warrants still be enforced by the police?

It is the same system and the culture of showing an arrest warrant is not there, from what I have seen since working on human rights (and what is online).

But if a politically motivated warrant was issued then, say against a JeI person, say 5 years ago, and not executed then, would that warrant still stand now, or would the government intervene and withdraw it?

During the Hasina regime, they could take anyone without an arrest warrant. That was the basic procedure for cases under AL. As far as I know, the BNP has not used that as a tactic. It is an institution, not in a political office. The warrant is in the system, because it’s the same police.

However, JeI is not facing problems at the moment. The only people facing a problem at the moment are the AL, although they are not facing that much trouble either. Because if you follow the statistics, extrajudicial killing, torture in custody, it is not there.

Would you have any statistics?

Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) and Odhikar maintain data related to human rights violations. These are the human rights-based organisations.

As far as I know, those who were arrested for participating in the July [2024] protests have all been released.

However, there have been other concerning incidents since the uprising. For example, a Baul folk singer was arrested after receiving threats. The authorities said they detained him for his own protection because they believed he could be attacked if he remained outside custody. This reflects broader concerns about the inability of law enforcement to provide effective protection.

[This information was added after the meeting There have also been attacks on artists, filmmakers, and religious shrines, raising concerns about freedom of expression and public safety. With the Awami League largely absent from politics, a political vacuum has emerged, and there are concerns that more radical groups are becoming more active. The key challenge is ensuring that law enforcement can effectively protect people’s rights and maintain public order.]

Are there any July 2024 protesters still in custody or have they all been released?

The protesters, they are all released now. Also, the IG gave the indemnity to the protesters, and I don’t think there are any still detained.

For protesters now, is there a police response?

Under the AL, alternative to policing came from the Army, they militarised and killed people. Police don’t kill people, it is more controlling. They used pellet guns, stun grenades, and tear gas. In the July [2024] uprising so many people were killed because of that practice. Now I observe the government trying to get away from that. In the IG they didn’t use these things but they used water cannons.

In BNP times, no mass protests have happened yet. But we have to see, since the Police Reform Commission has not been implemented yet, I’m not sure yet what the police response will be if there is a huge protest. That’s why it’s important. After 15 years of militarisation of the police, the commitment to change has to been there. However, at this moment I haven’t seen force. A few arrests have happened due to criticising the PM, a few cases have been filed on that.

The government sometimes didn’t take it very seriously and I believe they should be accountable for that.

Is there violence between or within political parties, and if so, is there a difference in levels pre-election and post-election?

In the last [2026] election, I did not witness much violence, it was handled well since the AL did not participate. So, the good part is it didn’t happen, the bad part is that it might still happen. The system is not fixed; it is still a broken system.

Has there been any state violence under the IG or under the new government?

Yes, political violence has happened throughout the last 2.5 years, a few incidents took place, but not that many have died. Obviously even one person is too many, it is not about the number, a family has lost their loved one if anyone has died. The IG tried to minimise that, the system was very vulnerable, but they did try really hard to get away from that practice.

[This information was added after the meeting According to Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), there were 35 alleged extrajudicial killings between August 2024 and July 2025.]

Are NGOs able to operate?

At this particular moment, there are no barriers. It’s a new government, we have to observe them.

What about the independence of the judiciary?

Interview with Rasheda K Choudhury, Executive Director for the Caretaker Government and Executive Director for the Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE)

Date: 14 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Rasheda K Choudhury, Former Advisor to the Caretaker Government and Executive Director for the Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE); 3 CPIT officials

Please can you provide us with some background about your role in your organisation and current priorities?

I am a campaigner, I call a spade a spade, I work for women’s rights and human rights.

Our organisation was established more than 35 years ago. The first education conference in Jomtien, Thailand, in 1990, was where the ‘education for all’ declaration was adopted. Some of our civil society leaders were there. We had military rule at that time, and we were in front of a global audience, decision makers from the UN and multi-lateral agencies. Bangladesh had 12 civil society organisations there, and the military ruler at the time was there. When he was asked to attend, he asked them who he should invite, one from the local or grassroots, you don’t have a platform, so they accepted this as a challenge. All the big names in education, non-state actors, 15 big agencies formed a platform in 1991, it was a voluntary platform and everyone contributed.

FITB [FutureEd Institute of Business & Technology] is regional organisation, supported by the FCDO, is well-known for its education programmes, so it was a completely voluntary initiative. We grew one year, then secured funding and OXFAM funding came in, then we started working, and the constitution was agreed. We started working in particular areas, especially in education and culture. We could feel the heat of extremist groups coming into education, so that’s why we were very careful. We had included Catholic groups and faith-based groups, but other groups didn’t want to be under our umbrella. It became 15 groups under our umbrella, and BRAC guided this organisation, then at one point in time they became elevated by CEDAW, then they wanted to have someone, not somebody voluntary, but a CEO to be recruited, then I was invited to join.

I was working for UNICEF as a consultant on gender issues, my specialisation is in gender issues. I was part of the research at the Education Institute of Dhaka University. When I was invited to join they asked me to look at the organisational mandate and make suggestions so they could amend the constitution. I challenged them that it needs to be open and broad-based, including teacher groups, that’s how it evolved. Now we have the membership of 172 NGOs, from BRAC to local community-based organisations.

To be a member there is criteria. Education must be in the mandate, they must be registered as a legal entity and have 3 years of operation. This is part of our governance structure and now through that process NGOs can express interest.

After 2005, we realised we needed to include teacher groups but teachers were not interested in being part of a NGO body, so they can be affiliate members and others are fee-paying voting members.

Then came other stakeholders after. Sustainable development groups, aid groups, private sector, non-profit organizations are not part of a big umbrella body. There are other groups and entities who prefer to be part of the network but not to be a voting member. So we have a slot for private sector bodies and 2 slots for provisional bodies. BRAC elects it own representatives.

We have 4 primary functions:

Coordination and networking

Capacity building of our partners

Research and dissemination

Advocacy – social networking etc

As a civil society organisation, has there been any change in your ability to function say under the Awami League era, under the IG, and now?

Yes, we follow 3 fundamental principles, we say non-negotiable principles:

Education is a fundamental human right

It is a state responsibility

We don’t want to be part of any government plans, we need our independence to work independently.

So, that’s where we sometimes came into conflict, for example we had a flagship programme, Education Watch, every year we publish on the basis of empirical, scientific data, both quantitative and qualitative data. So that is the Education Watch group, with 50 plus members. Multilateral agencies are also involved. Whenever we produced those reports, we used to run into conflict with the government, because of the data. It is the research that is saying nothing is happening inside the classroom, and that more students are going to faith-based schools like madrassas, and they didn’t want to accept it. Our principle was that we would not go for any government funding at any time, or our independence would not be there. Often, they refused to come to our meetings, it was a love-hate relationship otherwise. We used to complement or supplement programmes, like bringing in stakeholders to our workshops, or if they requested that we attend meetings/workshops we would do it.

Our role is to promote education but most of the time, because of our stance on data-based findings, and our policy options that we used, they wouldn’t accept that. The other one was at a local level, related to male governance. Local level, 170 plus members, used to see a lot of rent-seeking [CPIT addition: a situation wherein people or organisations exploit their position for personal gain[footnote 24]] from local authorities. We still have provisions in the regulations act that local administrators need to get a no objective certificate from local administrators before applying for the next funding cycle from, for example, the FCDO. There is a lot of rent seeking, we could not do anything at the national level and at the local level, local partners were harassed. It was not part of a political thing, but politics promoted that kind of rent seeking. It is part of the picture of male governance.

I was advisor to the last caretaker government, in 2007 and 2008. It was not because of a revolution, but because of turmoil in the political sector. Parliament was called again and the BNP decided to form of the caretaker government to supervise the elections. There was a lot of resistance from the political parties but we were invited to be part of that community. The military backed the caretaker government. It was very peaceful and there was no mob violence like during the IG this time.

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

At that time, the steam was building up among young people, you could feel it, in terms of employment, and them having a job quota for their favoured ones. So they came out in the streets, and the (then) PM had an emergency meeting with some civil society leaders who were close to her and she was challenged because she said ‘of course I will be giving a quota to these kids and their grandparents because they fought for Bangladesh, they are not razakars’ (collaborators with Pakistan in 1971). So, that was the trigger point, in the evening, it was not the mainstream students, but from the women’s halls, all the women came down on the streets and said ‘who am I? I am a collaborator’ like the PM said. The women came first and it was still peaceful. It spread to all the halls of residences of the university. Then it was peaceful, but the next day, the law enforcement agencies started, not only tear gas, but it was like in Myanmar, Sudan, they started killing. Then people from the general masses, they came out and joined the student movement, thousands of people were on the streets of Dhaka, because they were seeing that people were getting killed just because they were on the streets. People were unarmed.

One mother I still remember, called me the next day asking ‘what should I do?’ She lives in an apartment block on a main road. She was trying to get the windows shut because of tear gas and her daughter who was a 4th grader saw for herself the military killing people. This created trauma and the mother was asking me what to do. I don’t know her but she knew me through links.

And then came student leaders, it was so hurriedly done, and there was no backing from law enforcement agencies who were very much loyal to the then PM. The change was not only sudden, but to be very frank created a lot of turmoil because some people were hurriedly inducted to part of the decision [part of the IG]. The IG that formed, under Dr Muhammad Yunus, was a shell of the old and the new government but it was a government of necessity, that we had to have that government.

I saw myself a copy of a letter on the 5th August [2024] from the PM [Sheik Hasina]’s secretariat, her military advisor and the principal secretary that they had asked the PM for guidance on demonstrations. She wrote in Bangla to shoot on sight and kill. I saw this myself. How could an elected PM order this kind of thing? I asked the human rights mission to assist. Over 1,400 were killed.

So, we accepted this IG. The general people and the new young leaders were created. The younger people were raising funds for the one third of Bangladesh that was affected by floods because of climate change. After 2 months, people discovered that most of the money donated had gone here and there, not on what it was supposed to. That started creating an environment where people were not relying on the government’s stance on anything. Dr Yunus was a good, committed person, he wanted to do good, but he was not a politician, he could not control the young leaders. This was the worst part of the cabinet. There was lots of bureaucracy. Then there was the rise of extremist and far-right groups.

Far-right groups protested to the government. For example, talking about teachers in school, maybe music teachers, then through circulars they would protest and then the teacher would be removed. We asked, what’s wrong with sports teachers or music teachers? We challenged two advisors and asked why did you remove teachers, and they said they would raise questions but they said it came from the bureaucracy. We were frustrated, there were many CSOs and people in the IG who were close to us and we expected more but they could not control the mob culture. Education activists were being terrorised by these young students, even a female headteacher was abused. The mob culture was taking off and the IG would not do anything about it

What was the police reaction?

The IG were telling us that they instructed the police, but the police were demoralised and not willing to do anything, and then military weren’t interested to partake in anything.

Under the military supervision in 2008, we conducted the best ever, free and fair elections. It was globally proclaimed. We had the first national identification cards, the first time these were introduced was with the help of the military. It has become empowering to rural women because they don’t have passports. This is being used for business, just this photo ID, we introduced that in 2008.

The military was out of the scenario under the IG and the mob culture lasted for a long period.

What is this BNP government’s commitment to reform?

I think the fault also lies with the IG, because they could have done it. The Women’s Reform Commission, they were humiliated, we had to demonstrate on the streets, protecting those commissions, the IG could not provide that. People started asking whether they were really interested in getting those reforms in place. The IG also created a consensus commission, but even the formation of the commissions, even the consensus commission, didn’t have one single woman there. We protested this whole attitude of men, neglecting the gender equality thing. I was so frustrated because Dr Yunus was the promoter of women’s rights at the local level but he didn’t even notice it. So it happened, the commissions’ reports were mostly articulated in the forms of different ordinances. So most of the ordinances, other than 16, were passed by the parliament and came to effect as laws or acts, but the remaining ones, like the independence of the judiciary, civil society has problems in accepting why these did not go forward. It was a shock for us from this new government. And the independence of the anti-corruption commission, and the human rights commission, they were ignored totally. That was the first shock from this parliament.

We have to accept that this government got an absolute majority. The leader of the current government, he lived in London. Looking at his reflections, his attitude, his body language, it looks like he has learned it from a democracy like yours, that is good. Many of us we were really not expecting this kind of attitude from him. Because the leader had started doing it, others had followed. The marginal communities, then it spreads. The election manifesto, it’s a good one, but now they are trying to implement it [July Charter] from manifesto commitments which is confusing.

Anyway, it is a very good budget, there are lots of commitments, but balancing it with the balance sheet, this is where we have our concerns, but the priorities are right. We have been demanding education to be prioritised, and it is the 2nd of 10 priorities. The first is removing inequalities from all sectors, the 2nd is education, and the 3rd is health. So we have been demanding a roadmap for implementation, the other is governance. Still there is lots of rent-seeking going on, but it is nonsense, they are not in a position to control it, it looks like, despite their commitments. There are also calls for digitalisation.

You touched on the independence of the judiciary, what is your sense of that now, particularly in relation to any politically-motivated trials?

In terms of people going to trial, there was a lot of mishandling of the cases because all those young people went to the police station and lodged a complaint of ‘this person killed someone’ during the protests, so the accuser used to get the upper hand. Sometimes the media actually printed the cases with the name of the petitioner, they didn’t even know that he or she was fighting that case, that kind of fraud or error happened, after the election period.

Many were arrested, some of them got out on bail. Even some AL ministers, one was well known for their integrity, and had never been a person linked to anything bad, let alone murder, and he was accused of killing someone in their constituency, so people lost confidence in the trial. Even the party is saying we can’t do anything about it because that case was not filed by us. It is a tricky scenario now. Others like the politicians, those cases where there was a lot of corruption, those were true actually, like the order during the protests to shoot, and the police army because of the abduction cases. People were abducted suddenly and never came back, under Hasina, but the question is a fair trial, whether they are getting it or not, where is the evidence, so this is where we are stuck now as a nation.

To summarise the Bangladesh issue, at this point in time we need to gain credibility and create confidence among its partners, especially in the global north. At the same time, the global south, we are having issues with India. Myanmar and Nepal are not a problem. But with India we are having issues because of their political scenario and groups.

There are right-wing groups there, we should say that we feel that this government is neither right not left wing but trying to follow a moderate policy, that is what their motto is at this time, supposedly.

Yesterday I was talking to the Women’s Affairs and Social Welfare Minister. We tried to give them suggestions, but they can’t make these at the moment, it is not possible for them to amend the constitution. We suggested they should have a framework, to bring all education under one Act but they are not sure about it at the moment. Over all these years, what we feel as civil society is to look at the picture at a more rural level, how groups are claiming their space within the broader family, rural areas etc., and the Middle Eastern culture, they have brought in their culture, and their families are very much influenced in their dress, attitudes and everything. I said this is your fault, you have been working so hard on the revolution to notice that they [other groups] are taking over your space. A lot of political workers have been trying to help women with health tips, even going door to door to help them, even with family planning. Like Dr Yunus, they said this is our failure, we allowed them to capture the civil society democratic space, but now we are realising and it may not be too late. The first issue should be gender.
