2024 changed some people’s needs in Bangladesh. Everyone is very involved with politics here. Even the tea maker in village markets in his store is talking about politics. They do their morning prayers, come out of the mosque and they discuss politics. In the evening they watch the TV screens in the tea stalls together and sip on their tea and discuss politics. People are very involved in politics in Bangladesh. And with mobile phones, everyone knows what is going on, especially with fake news, and on social media. So, whatever is happening in Dhaka, everyone knows. The priorities have changed for the people, they don’t just want food on the table anymore, people want more.

Someone approached me for funding for a local mosque in the village from government funds and they were asking for air con which is a luxury. People want more and they want luxury, expectations are high and patience is low.

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

The political environment hasn’t changed. The environment is still very vibrant and people’s expectations of the politicians are very high. But the political people have changed. The environment of corruption is still there, not everywhere and not to the extent that it was before, that was beyond corruption. It has come down some notches now. Our Prime Minister is being very stern and having zero tolerance for corruption. For example, the budget for food in the PM’s office is 100 Taka, so it’s a small, simple meal. That is the way he is now trying to promote Bangladesh, he wants us to be frugal. So, this has changed within the political spectrum. We also have to politically correct ourselves.

How have the changes since then affected the political groups?

I think all political parties can now operate freely. None of us could operate freely before. I think the first term of the Hasina government, from 2008 to 2014 was liveable but the election in December 2014 was a total sham. In 2014 government was formed with uncontested seats and everything went downwards. So, from 2014 onwards, Bangladesh saw a change and I wouldn’t call that politics, it was more like a dictatorship. It wasn’t a government anymore, it was one woman, one word. So, our whole politics changed.

I hope politics in this country has changed for the better and never goes back to the authoritarian rule of the Hasina Regime.

We have our problems, of course, that cannot be eradicated in one day. When you have 10 years of bad politics, it takes a little time to get it back to some form of normality.

Yesterday in parliament there was a big skirmish between members, and there was uproar, but this is what you want in politics. Some of our MPs were a little ‘OTT [over the top]’, they were beating the table, shouting, and standing up etc, but that’s what you want in parliament.

We still have to wait and see how parliament functions, so far it is okay.

What is the BNP’s relationship with JeI now that they are the opposition?

It is interesting, in 2008, when we were in opposition, I used to go to parliament to watch from the opposition side and sit in the box in the gallery. Members used to debate, and opposition used to have walk outs. What I saw outside of the chamber, in the lobby, was that people were not so friendly. The situation was always a little tense. That has changed. What I see now is that when they come out into the lobby from the main parliament area (there are different lobbies; women have a lobby together whether in opposition or government they have tea and snacks together, but men have separate lobbies for opposition and government). So, I have not been to the men’s side but the women, we do not have any problems, we are sitting and eating together. Even outside the lobby, I’ve seen people talking together, so it is a much better environment.

I’ve been to Westminster many times and seen people in the members’ restaurant, everyone is sitting together, and that is a similar atmosphere to what I am seeing here now, this is a healthy environment for democracy.

JeI is always threatening us [that they will] walk out but we talk to them, we are saying let’s not go back to olden days. Let us work together and let’s move forward. So we’ll see what happens.

In terms of the reforms proposed by the interim government, what is the progress with reform now?

The reforms have been discussed because we did sign the Charter (with a note of dissent). Reform has to come but it has to come with legality. It can’t be signed as a Charter and then be made law. We just now had the budget, and the budget is waiting to be approved. What we need now is for each point of the Charter to come up in parliament, for debate and then for a vote, like the laws that were enacted recently. When you are in a democratic system, the bills need to come through the parliament for a vote. The Referendum said yes, but the Referendum was so confusing for people. We wanted the Referendum as well, so that we have the people’s vote to go ahead and implement these laws. But to implement these laws, you need to make it into law. If you want to make it into law, you have to come and vote in parliament. I think we will do it, and the reforms will become law. We won’t just say this is a reform.

One question that was always there was, is Yunus’ government legal, can they do reforms or not? So, one of the things from our government is that we want to make these reforms lawful.

There was the idea of women going into reserved seats, maybe 50 to 100, and many people thought that was great. I’d love that, however, I prefer elected women parliamentarians rather than reserved seats. If we could give 33% of nominations to women, I would prefer that. But it is difficult in rural areas of Bangladesh to campaign because some areas don’t even have any roads. Maybe in the future it will be better.

We have 50 women’s seats at the moment, and they are very active, including the women in JeI alliance. They have 14 women. We are all functioning. We are all participating and are standing up to present ourselves. If they want to say things, they are saying it, it’s lovely, and that is what we want. We are trying to encourage women to participate in the local elections, because that will be the route under which we can bring more women to parliament.

In the local election there are 3 unions, and each one has about 9 wards. Out of the 9 wards there will be 3 women contesting, so there will be one woman for every 3 wards. Let’s see how many women come through from the local elections.

In terms of members and supporters of different political groups, are they able to openly attend demonstrations and protest now?

Yes, they are able to protest. In Bangladesh, outside a polling station, for example, we have hundreds of people, they call it a festival, I call it a commotion. Election day is a bit like going to the airport to see someone off in Bangladesh, everyone is there, they are all out in the street, it is like a festival. The interesting part is you’re not supposed to feed them, the voters, but who is going to stop them, they are all having food.

During the pre-election period, were there political protests?

We didn’t have many protests this time, but we did have some skirmishes between JeI and us (BNP), but there were very few isolated incidents and they were not bad. We had EU observers, who came and did a report which covered prior to the election and after the election. I was invited by the EU to a meeting after the election. I was representing the BNP, and there was JeI, NCP, and the Electoral Commission, and we had these discussions and we agreed that there were skirmishes during the election period, but they weren’t significant. The EU did an extensive report which was very positive.

In the post-election period, once the BNP was in government, what about the situation then, was there any political violence?

As I said, there has been one or two, but not really.

Sources noted a breakdown in law and order during the [2024] uprisings, and then the IG came in. What is the situation now with law and order, and with police capacity and capability?

There are two things we find very tough. One of the biggest issues is drugs, and we have also seen some very horrible scenarios of the rape of young girls. But this was happening before as well, so this is not something new. So, it’s not a case of the new government has come in and that has happened.

There was the case during the Hasina regime in Madaripur of a 12-year-old who was raped by her brother-in-law, her brother-in law’s-father, and her brother-in-law’s brother, and this was supervised by the brother-in-law’s mother. She died. This was horrific and it comes from a culture that was unfortunately brought in by the previous government.

I said in 2008, to some US observers and diplomats, who went to observe the 2008 election, that the culture I have seen is that the BNP is known to be a party of higher cultured and of more educated people, people who have been in politics for generations, such as retired officers and retired bureaucrats. The AL was a worker’s party, Sheikh Mujib was a worker, he was never educated himself, he was from the Shamik Muslim League. A lot of the top politicians that were in the AL although they had very seasoned politicians, but they all came from the background of ‘muscle power’. So, they are two different set-ups. The AL, for the last 10 years they became very powerful, and they really were going round and doing things that destroyed our country. So, to take them out of the muscle power system, it will take time, it won’t be overnight.

Drugs have flooded everywhere now, but it is a global problem, but in this country and the region. Poverty is there still, and drugs are an excuse to get out of poverty. So, we need to do a lot of rehabilitation.

One of the things I am not happy with is when people are sentenced to death. But the law of the country is sentenced to death in cases like with the rapes and killing. This happened just a couple of weeks ago with the Ramisa case. Even the wife of the rapist was involved. They had to be sentenced to death. It’s disgraceful that individuals will commit such heinous crimes. My question is what kind of pleasure does someone get out of these crimes? However, these things are happening quite a lot and the criminals have to be punished accordingly.

I’ve dealt with abuse cases as well in the UK, there are sick people in this world. We can’t just stop these sick things that happen in the world, but we need to work towards it getting better. The drug problem in Bangladesh has predominantly come from the culture of India. One of the things we have to remember is that, religiously, these things, like drinking alcohol, they are forbidden in our culture. So, these things are hidden. Of course there are people who drink alcohol, but it is not done in the open. But in India it is their culture, they do these things within their religions, they drink and use drugs for pujas [Hindu ritual], so culturally it is acceptable. But in predominantly Muslim countries as in Bangladesh, it is not acceptable.

I don’t know which way we have to go, for example, in the Netherlands I think marijuana was legalised, so it was treated like cigarettes. We as Muslims can’t make this legal. We have to find ways to stop this kind of criminal activities be it drugs or other offences.

Interview with Bangladesh Police

Date: 15 June 2026

Location: Police Headquarters, Dhaka

Present: 4 police officials; 3 CPIT officials; 2 FCDO officials

What are the current policing challenges and what are your priorities?

Under the new government, there are many socioeconomic issues which bring many problems. There are unemployment issues, that is the buzzing problem of the day. The new government has had many tests and trials with the economic situation, but they are doing their best. Recently, there have been two big religious festivals, and we have been able to maintain law and order during these. In general, we are maintaining the law-and-order situation to the best level. If you are talking about the capital Dhaka, at times the population can exceed more than 40 to 50 million. People use Dhaka as part of their journey from one part of the country to another and will have a short stay. This can contribute to traffic pressure and the number of people living in housing. It is a very busy city. So, there are a number of problems. Environmental issues contribute to city life, law and order and unemployment. If there is too much rain, in the rainy season, it contributes to waterlogging and traffic, and people can lose employment.

Overall, we have been able to maintain law and order. There were a lot of political cases which didn’t seem to be accurate. We agreed with our Ministry of Home Affairs to form a District Committee, which would allow someone who thought they had a false case to appeal to the committee who would look into matters. If it was found to be unjust then the Committee could recommend withdrawal of the case.

Are these cases lodged under the Hasina regime?

Yes, and soon after the AL’s departure there were some cases registered during the student uprising. You can always register a case, but it is during the time of investigation that it will be revealed true or false. Someone can claim a case is false and malicious, he can appeal to a District Committee, and they will decide to recommend it to MoHA to withdraw.

What is the legal status of arrest warrants if they have not been executed?

The arrest warrant is a part of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It remains valid until it is put into action. There are some exceptions; if the person goes to court and receives bail, the warrant is withdrawn because they have already appeared before court, or if someone is dead, or if any cases are withdrawn, that is the usual disposal. Some people have had cases withdrawn even if they haven’t appealed, but if the person did not go to the court then the arrest warrant is not withdrawn, so they have to proceed to the court to ask for it to be withdrawn. If a person goes to court with a recommendation for the case to be withdrawn they can keep a copy of that with them, so they have it in case law enforcement go to their house, so it can be mitigated but they have to go the court to get it withdrawn. We do not have the system in place to share this between police stations. This is the process. But even if someone is apprehended and taken to the court, he can show the papers to the court that the case has been withdrawn and they will be released.

Is there a difference in procedure between different areas of Bangladesh?

Our criminal justice system is same everywhere, metropolitan areas, all the same.

Are the [computer] systems connected between different police areas?

We have the Crime Data Management System (CDMS) which is accessible to all investigation officers.

If a police officer doesn’t follow procedure or is found to be complicit in corruption or human rights abuses, what happens, what is the procedure?

If someone does not act under the purview of law, it is an individual responsibility, it is an individual liability and a matter of discipline.

Is there a mechanism for victims of crime to report police who have not taken their case seriously?

Of course, he can go to the higher ups, even if he is wrongly fined in the streets, he can appeal to the deputy commissioner. There cannot be a despotic attitude in the police. Human rights are very important. The Bangladesh Police have been contributing to operations around the world. I’m sure you understand the political situation, but our police have a good reputation in keeping order in society. Sometimes with the nature of the environment here, you have to be cruel to be kind.

Does a person’s political opinion affect someone’s ability to seek protection from the police?

Any individual can seek assistance from the police, he can go and file a case regarding troubles he faces, and the local police definitely will give him support and care; grievances will be addressed. There are different types of cases, if you look at the registers of the police stations, for what kind of cases they receive each day. When too many people live in a small area, differences will come up. It is how society tolerates it, tolerance and justice are the backbone of a society.

Look at the incidents that took place in Belfast and the [UK] stabbing case, the Nowak case, he said I cannot breathe and a few minutes later the man died. There were allegations against the police because he was handcuffed when he said I can’t breathe. You understand, the police have to work under stress in society, it is a stressful job. In our country, there are socioeconomic problems, we will get complaints, otherwise no one would be able to work. You understand that the police are a shock absorber of society, everyone complains. We understand that there are limitations too, so you have to go through the society in a ‘test and trial’ process. There are many complaints: theft, mugging, rapes. There are very few incidents of food insecurity nowadays as many people now have produced crops in good amounts, but there are cases of land litigation, business fraud, and forgery.

If someone, for example, from Jel, had a political dispute with the community in their area, would they be able to seek police protection and what measures are in place for impartiality?

As I told you, whatever political identity you have, everyone is equal. I’m sure you are aware of political developments; I don’t want to comment because I am a professional and deal with matters professionally. If there is an incident, we go by the book and go by the code of criminal procedure. Whatever political opinions they have, it doesn’t make a difference. However, if someone [in the police] goes beyond and is delinquent, that is their individual responsibility. But anyone can solicit help from the police.

How do you foresee implementation of reform after the [July 2024] uprising?

It is not easy to change everything overnight. Every incident has some echoes. We had 16/17 years of rule by the previous government which left behind legacies. So, we are not able to change everything overnight. It is a continuous process. One thing that is very important is tolerance; you have to have tolerance. Political parties have to practice it. If political parties have mutual respect for each other, this will trickle down to other members of society, and everyone will learn. About reforms, no one wants to venture into reform because they think about the consequences. It is natural for people to be resistant to change in the system because they have fear of the unknown. Another thing is good governance and having quality people. Confidence comes from knowledge and knowledge comes from learning. If there aren’t the right people, in the right places, then you cannot deliver.

Regarding police reform, we cannot reform by ourselves because we are controlled by the Ministry of Home Affairs, we are under their umbrella. If you talk about overall reform, there has to be a democratic system. Appointments, transfers and promotions should be fair, and the system should be based on merit and talent.

How would you describe the police response to instances of political violence after the uprising?

The response is good. I’m sure you understand that during the uprising police officers sacrificed their lives. It has had an impact on the police, and we are trying to recover. You have to understand that when you face trauma, you need time before you can go back out. Being in the police is a job where you need the support of the local people, and people need to have confidence in the police. Whatever the problem is in people’s houses, whether a gas leak, fire, they approach the police station first, so they definitely have confidence, maybe their expectations are too high. Close to 800 people have one police officer, this is on average, across the country.

The overall criminal justice system, I personally believe it has to be given due attention, because the access to justice should be equal. If there are allegations against someone, there should be a speedy investigation and trial, because if he is found innocent and it takes 2 years, then he will have a lot of harassment in his life; whether they are working, a student, or otherwise occupied, this is a pressure. You might be excluded from jobs. The police alone can’t do anything, other stakeholders need to be involved, prison management and the judicial system should come under one umbrella to manage. If a witness goes to court to give witness and the judge is not available that day or the prosecutor is not available, what happens is that they have to come to court another day. Sometimes a witness can’t come on a different day, and then it will delay the criminal justice procedure. We have to have some mechanism so that proceedings are completed within the least possible time.

What is the progress of cases in relation to abuses under the Hasina regime of officials? Sources note there are the ICT trials, but do you know about lower-level cases?

Yes, the cases filed during the Sheikh Hasina government, 21,585 cases have already been withdrawn as we came to know.

They were accused of crimes under that government?

Yes, they were found to be false.

Were these politically-motivated cases?

Yes. More cases have been examined, and more cases will be withdrawn, I believe.

CPIT clarified the original question: What about the arrest of officials that were in the AL government/acting on its behalf? We know about the trials at the ICT, but are there domestic trials?

Well, it depends from man to man, and on whatever offence they have committed. You come across a lot of events in the daily newspaper, some people who were connected to the previous government, and who had important roles during the uprising, oppressing, harassing people, have been brought to justice.

The criminal justice system, you can always complain, you can always go to the court, whichever police station, but when you go to court, to prove an offence, there needs to be enough evidence. Sometimes there is not enough evidence, because of a lack of evidence the crimes can’t be proved. This happens everywhere. Sometimes the offence is true, sometimes the grievance is higher than the offence itself, these are the issues we come across. Those who have played roles in torturing people have been brought to justice and they are facing trials now. Of course, in the trial the offences may be proved or not proved.

Your colleague was going to give some statistics?

Another Police HQ official: 21,585 cases withdrawn.

There have been recommendations by the government, from district level or committee which we have in metropolitan areas. We believe it has given relief to 500,000 individuals. It’s a continuous process and recommendations are still coming to districts, magistrates or the committee, to withdraw cases.

Could you explain the process to get cases withdrawn?

You go to the district committee and appeal to district level. You put in a plea for withdrawal and they will examine the allegations.

Who raises this issue? Does the government identify these cases?

Another Police HQ official: An accused person or their relatives may apply to have their warrant withdrawn.

We have a well-structured procedure. The accused person or relative may apply to the district. We have 64 districts, 64 committees. At district level, the application is reviewed within 15 working days through the public prosecutor. If it is identified as politically-motivated, or harassment-related, we withdraw the case, then a recommendation is forwarded to the Ministry of Home Affairs. Then if it goes back to the district magistrate, to the court, the court issues an order, and the process is complete and comes to an end.

How does the police operate in terms of central control, is there central control over the local forces?

We haven’t been able to change much of the administration that the UK left, neither did India or Pakistan, because it was so well structured. If you look at history, it is not easy to change as there are lot of pillars and if we take out one, the whole system would collapse. There is only one national police, the Bangladesh Police, and then we have divisions. Some of the districts fall under the division. Each division has a Deputy Inspector General, he looks after law and order, but he has to report to us directly at the HQs as well. So whatever directives he receives, the other Inspector Generals also receive, it is the same whether it is the metropolitan area, or beyond the metropolitan area. It is all the same in the committee.

What are your current policing priorities, going forward?

Like any other country, I personally believe, you cannot have any other option other than the rule of law as the main objective of a police force. When you establish the rule of law, then you can establish human rights and other issues. It sounds easy to pronounce the rule of law, but in practice, in a country like ours which is infested with problems, it is not easy. You have to treat people equally; everyone should have equal access to justice and facilities and if you fail to provide that then resentment goes up. Rule of law is best.

Secondly, women’s empowerment. It is very important because 50% of the total population are women. Many now are working ladies, some are housewives who stay within rural areas. In urban areas, most women work. You have to take care of women and give preference to them within the system. We have to have positive discrimination; if a man and a woman are found equal, then the woman should be given preference as part of the empowerment policy, you have to empower women, this is very important. These issues will follow the rule of law, and you must have that first as the single motto at the head of all police forces. If you establish that, the better society goes too.

Are there any official statistics on arrest numbers collated by the police, for politically-motivated reasons, is that tracked?

We do not have any statistics on politically-motivated arrests, we cannot say that. This is the language of newspapers, media, social media. We work under a lot of pressure, and this has to be taken into account. We have to be allowed to work freely, without influence. Our police cannot function in the way that UK police function. If someone influences me to go beyond the law then the onus of that bargain falls onto my shoulders. We cannot say we have done it under duress or under the influence of someone, that is an individual choice. If someone goes beyond that, it is his personal responsibility.

Some NGOs tracked pre-election violence and violent incidents between party members, I’m just wondering if you have comparable information?

No.

Are we able to look at a blank arrest warrant, to see what it looks like? Do they look the same all across the country?

We can show you one. It is the same across the country, it has been and goes back to 1898 when it started. We have incorporated some Bengali words in lieu of English but some English words are still there, that is what you left. It is also available on the internet.

Interview with Senior Fellow of Practice, BRAC Institute of Governance and Development

Date: 15 June 2026

Location: British High Commission, Dhaka

Present: Senior Fellow of Practice, BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD); 1 CPIT official; 2 FCDO officials

How has the political environment changed since August 2024?

It’s quite a long period of time. Looking back, at the beginning, it was hard to know what was going on; what was being said and what was not being said. There were a lot of rumours, so it was very difficult to assess what was happening. We [BIGD] were very interested from the beginning. There were promises of democracy. We are interested in social movements and governance, and we were following the process to understand youth involvement in the [July 2024] uprising. Youth social movements led the uprising and we wanted to understand what their role was. It wasn’t so clear on how political groups got involved and to what extent. Some of this came out later. On the front it was a spontaneous, youth-led movement. However, it was not so spontaneous as there was some organising behind it. We were interested to see who these groups were.

At the beginning, the youth didn’t say they were a political party/affiliated, they said it was an anti-discrimination movement. It then transferred to the citizen’s platform and then into the NCP. After this, we began to see who remained and who dropped out. From a gender perspective, there was strong participation of young women in the anti-discrimination movement. Then they began to be sidelined and then they dropped out altogether from September [2024]. It was a matter of concern for us. At the beginning, I tried to interview some of the young women to see how they came into their role, and to capture what they did before they disappeared from the movement. Some didn’t want to speak; some were willing to talk and some of the most visible figures stayed on the national media.

There were a lot of organisations interested in hearing stories about women’s role in the anti-discrimination movement. Some activists were more visible than others, some went back to their studies and families, some remained active in BRAC and Dhaka University.

The women’s rights group, Naripokkho, held meetings and consultations, bringing in young women to find out what’s on the pulse and what could be done for the women’s movement.

Now that everyone is talking about the anti-discrimination movement, it would be a good time to put through the agenda for women’s equality, but we found this faced a lot of resistance. With the opening of the civic space, there was a lot more space for right wing groups and conservative views and organisations to add their views. This led to some protest and they countered what was being said by the Left or the women’s movement. In some cases, it turned violent. The LGBTQI movement faced violence. The women’s movement faced backlash which was mainly online on social media. In some cases, women were harassed, some young girls or sex workers expressing themselves.

We thought, with the interim government, there would be more of a space for the women’s movement. The interim government set up reform commissions. I was part of the women’s affairs reform commission. It was a good opportunity to put an agenda in front of the interim government. We were promised a lot of reform. The whole anti-discrimination movement was saying they did not want a repeat of Sheikh Hasina. Everyone was talking about putting safeguards in place and reforms. There were different reform commissions, and we thought this would put ideas forward on what reforms needed to be done. In terms of transfer of power, we were very disappointed. The interim government couldn’t or wouldn’t take on the discussions from the reform commission and put them into law. The recommendations went to a consensus commission which political parties dominated. After this, the women’s rights agenda went backwards, and other issues. Women were not consulted and there was no space for women’s rights groups in the consensus commission. We found the space was starting to exclude. Jel were getting stronger, the Awami League was pushed out. The Awami League have done a lot of bad [things], but they have done some good things. Some progressive leaders couldn’t be named, even professionals that worked with the AL became persona non-grata and there was a lot of blacklisting.

[Under the interim government] there was political violence against AL supporters. A lot of people went into hiding. Their houses were ransacked and they were having to hide. There were a lot false cases. There were cases where 100 people were named and just because you were the 99th person on the list you were named in the case without evidence. So it was a difficult period.

There was a lot of extortion. Many went to jail from the AL or AL supporters. They would come out of prison if they paid huge amounts of money. Many took the opportunity to move against enemies. Even if it wasn’t for political reasons, they would use it as a chance to add people’s names to lists to be used in false cases. There were so many false cases, a lot of torture and a lot of bribery. One district advisor said they couldn’t file a case until it was vetted by a magistrate. There are a number of people [who were associated with the Awami League] I know that are still in hiding, some have left the country and some are in jail.

For those who managed to get bail, it was by spending a lot of money. For people dealing with prisoners, they have to pay the guards so much, around 1,000 to 5,000 taka, even to get put into the division for political prisoners you have to pay. David Bergman [Journalist] has documented this and has written about some of these cases. Even in the ICT, the prosecutors were asking for bribes. Mostly in the Awami League cases.

So it’s been difficult. Everyone is still hoping with the new government that things will improve and that the persecution of the Awami League will also stop. Under the interim government, the BNP was more about banning Awami League activities, not banning the party. At the local level, we have been interviewing female youth leaders. We have seen that people at the local level in political parties who know each are other providing protection. Also, some AL members have joined Jel or BNP and have been welcomed in. There has been a culture of compromise in local areas, people are often from the family [families connected to political parties], neighbourhood or have other close ties.

Are there examples of this happening in specific parts of country?

Yes. The BNP was a bit wary of taking in too many AL members, so maybe central leadership was not happy, but at the local level they’ve been absorbed into the party.

Government parties, whichever party comes to power, in terms of the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT), all talk about anti-discrimination and non-discrimination, but they haven’t done anything for the CHT. Recently, there was a bombing incident, and months later people in CHT communities have been arrested and put in jail, including children and pregnant women. CHT human rights leaders are threatened, and local tribal leaders are threatened when they speak out on issues. There is censorship.

Under which government?

Ever since I can remember. Ever since the military has been involved, no political government has tried to make changes. People often migrate from CHT and have gone to Australia and other countries where they have found it more welcoming.

Has the newly elected BNP government implemented any recommendations from commissions formed under the IG? If so, what?

That’s a sore point. Both Jel and BNP had discussed reform in their manifestos. The BNP are taking up some reform ideas.

In terms of the women’s reform commission and the recommendations suggested, the commission have tried to engage with the new government. At the beginning, they said they were so busy that they couldn’t take meetings. Then when you meet them at events, they tell us to come and speak to them. It feels like there is no real buy in. There was so much effort put into the commission. The interim government didn’t manage to do much to implement recommendations, it feels like a real loss of time and effort.

I’ll pass you a copy of report we have done on reform.

What is the role of the auxiliary organisations (particularly student wings) in political parties and what are their activities?

Student wings had elections at all universities. They seem to have been fair. People were quite worried that the Jel student wing came out strongly but maybe that is to be expected as they have been very good at organising. The BNP and AL wings were more about patronage and violence and not really working for the welfare of students. If you focus on student housing, scholarships, and student nutrition then the student wing is more likely to get votes. It is interesting to see how student leaders develop and enter the mainstream.

Our research on student politics found it was a training ground for political parties. It really teaches them how to organise, how to do public speaking, reach out and build relations with mainstream parties. There are a number of people in mainstream parties who came through student politics. There have been debates on whether student politics should be banned or encouraged. We need to have a democratic and safe culture of student politics. There needs to a more constructive culture with democratic norms, and less violence and asking for money and all of that. That’s a different debate on how you ensure that there is a healthy student politics – we have to figure that out.

Was there any violence during student wing elections?

There was not that much compared to before; it was very peaceful. There were minor incidents before they released the results. On the whole, it was very peaceful which shows it can be done.

What were the levels of pre-election/election period intra- and inter-party violence? How does this compare to levels under the AL?

What has been coming out from our interviews is that the official reporting of violence is much less than what took place. The election complaints mechanism didn’t work very well. You will see in the EU report, they did a survey which found that people didn’t know they had a complaint office in their location, didn’t know about them at all or they didn’t know they could complain.

In interviews, people said that when they did lodge a complaint they weren’t taken seriously or that they took the complaint and nothing happened.

In Dhaka, this was reported in national media, a Jel candidate made a violent statement against women. There was a complaint filed that the speech was promoting violence against women. It went to the Chief Election Commissioner and nothing happened. This was a public incident of violence, we thought that because it was done publicly there would be some impact but there was no action from the election commission.

There was an incident where a rape by [a] BNP [member] was reported in Hatia due to the woman voting for the NCP. In the end, there was no evidence found to support this claim.

Compared to other elections, it has been more peaceful, and I haven’t heard of many incidents of violence against minorities.

Some Jel candidates put a religious angle on the election. For example, saying if you want to go to heaven you have to vote for us. The central leadership denied this and we don’t know if they gave any instruction to do this, but it happened more in rural areas.

There were also allegations of vote buying. All parties, except for left wing parties, spent a lot of money on votes.

In the election, so few women were nominated. The left wing parties did the best compared to other parties, about one third or half of their candidates were women.

What was the police response during the elections?

When people complained, the police didn’t take it seriously. Even BNP candidates complained that there was police bias towards Jel, and independent candidates complained there was a bias toward larger parties. So, there was a lot of jockeying before [the] election. The interim government said local administrations at all levels, including district commissioners, would be neutral. There was some reshuffling and each party accused the other of putting in their people and that the local administrations were biased.

Another thing during the IG, they took all locally elected people out and administrative people were appointed by officials.

There is a problem with the whole politicisation of the local administration. Each new government when it comes in will recruit people who are party loyalists. They will have background checks, looking at family connections, etc. This also happened during the AL period, and Jel were discriminated against.

Recently, there was a huge purge in the police of those perceived to be affiliated with the AL. There was a new batch of police officers supposed to be sworn in after one year of training, and the whole ceremony was cancelled the day before.

Also, each party tries to win favour by protecting minorities, they want to buy loyalty. We will have to see what the BNP does.

[This information was added after the meeting The AL claimed that they would protect the Hindu minority. This resulted in many of the Hindu voters supporting them.]

What is the police response to protest? Are there differences to their response under the AL, the IG and now?

During the IG, we seemed to have protests all the time for anything. It was quite disruptive, every day there was some sort of protest. I think people felt it was safer to protest. During the AL period, you had to get permission for demonstrations or protests, so there were no direct political protests as they would have had trouble. It was ok for environmental or women’s rights protests, they were allowed. There were also LGBTQI protests under the AL.

During the IG, there were some parties supporting the IG. Some movements were very conservative and targeted any protests they thought came from the LGBTQI community.

Just a few days ago, they [LGBTQI activists] have gatherings every Friday in one of central places. This was published on social media, and they were attacked by religious groups, not by the police.

Now the police just stand and watch, they do not take action rather than attacking protestors. Under the AL, the police were joining AL leaders beating up Jel. After the elections we haven’t seen that kind of violence and I hope we won’t.

But if the AL, let’s say, makes itself visible on the streets, they would be at risk. There has been violence against the AL. Sheikh Hasina’s house has been burnt down, there have been repeated burnings and attacks on symbolic AL places where there is nothing. The anger is still there and that might erupt again. We are hearing rumours that the AL is trying to organise and put money back into the organisation. There was a fear around the election that the AL might cause disruption. A lot of that fear comes from the digital sphere and social media. In Bangladesh, people watch political channels associated with parties and hear different things which can create different perceptions of reality. There was rumour that there would be a massacre on a specific day or that Hasina would come back by a certain date.

Social media is emerging as form of political violence. Everything is at stake. For example, the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) criticised public servants wanting a pay hike under the new budget. This created such a strong reaction online. CPD staff were attacked online for their clothes, sari and haircuts. Some young research assistants, young women working there, when they go to seminars they dress nicely, and they are being attacked personally online for that.

Before the IG, BRAC had done research on online safety for young people and young online activists. This includes LGBTQI individuals. The BRAC event came under attack. We had to remove the event from Facebook. The LGBTQI individuals had to go into hiding. We have now had to change protocols, events are now closed-door, people are screened and invited.

During the IG, the head of the women’s reform commission had her photo printed off and people were throwing shoes at the picture. She received death threats and there was a dummy doll put up and beaten publicly.

Can NGOs/CSOs operate freely? Are there any legal or practical barriers?

During the AL, there was a culture of the detective branch and NS [national security] Intelligence coming to events in plain clothes to see if there was any anti-state activity. They considered women’s organisations as generally harmless and sort of open about what they are doing so they didn’t always come. Although, if we had people from Pakistan, the government would want to know. There is surveillance for NGOs who are receiving foreign funding, there is a clause that they can’t carry out anti-state activity without there being a definition of anti-state. Previously, they have suspended funding for BLAST and TIB [Transparency International Bangladesh]. In proposals submitted to the government, we would have to word things in way to make it clear we were not attacking the government.

Any kind of criticism was seen as attack, if we were talking about good governance, transparency and accountability. But we can use those words now and we can do real work. Although, we have seen that where organisations have been too critical, they won’t get invited to committees or meetings where draft law is being discussed. It happened under the AL. Under the new government, it is hard to say as they have been so busy settling down after being elected. The women’s reform commission have been trying to get an interview with the minister, but he hasn’t responded after 110 days, so does he think the subject matter is too hot to handle or is it not a priority? Although he has been going to other NGO events, and when they were in opposition they did mix with NGOs, so there is a working relationship there that we can build on.

Hopefully it will change under the new government. Trade union registration will become easier. The law has changed to allow those with smaller membership, whereas previously they had to pay a lot of bribes to get registration.

Under the IG we hoped corruption would go down but it didn’t.

Is there any update on those held for their actions under the Hasina regime? Are people still in custody? On what charges? At what stage of the process, i.e. proceeding towards trial?

In terms of accountability and justice, those who were disappeared and big cases going back to 2016 like the [Sohagi Jahan] Tonu case, a young girl who was raped and murdered by those in [the] army, [which] was swept under carpet, is now coming back. BNP or left political[ly] motivated cases like Taqi, a 14 year old killed by AL leaders, are coming back [under investigation].

There have been all these people disappeared. There was a commission that looked into this and the UN came in. Many people have still not been accounted for. People were held in isolation and in torture chambers. Two of these people who were forcibly disappeared have become MPs. These people have been released and rehabilitated but whether there will be justice for the people responsible for what happened to them we don’t know.

There have been some ICT hearings but we don’t know if anyone has been punished for their crimes, I’m not sure. Hasina and others carried out orders but it is not being addressed properly. Under the IG there were reformed rules for the ICT so that justice would be given in fairer way and follow different international standards. However, they are not following what has been agreed on in those rules and what there has been a discussion on. For example, charge sheets being delivered within a certain timeframe and if that’s not done then the person has to be released, they are not following that. Also, if people try to speak on behalf of the AL then they are labelled an AL supporter. They are getting labelled even though the press is supposed to be free, people like David Bergamn who are speaking out on the human rights of AL members.

Are there any barriers to freedom of movement, for example if an AL member encountered difficulties in their community could they relocate to a different area?

They have relocated. When we have been doing interviews, people from different political backgrounds, women from minority Dalit communities and others like that, who had been elected under the AL and seen as AL supporters, are no longer in this area. Some of the ones we contacted said that they can’t come and meet, a few we contacted said it’s better that we don’t come to meet them and that they can’t come to meet us as they are in hiding.

Others are much more open. They were previously with the AL but they are no longer with them as they have other identities, such as working with a NGO, even though people know they were elected to the local government as an AL supporter.

In one example, one of the women [associated with the AL] was attacked and was traumatised, her husband is depressed and their one son left. They said they will never do politics. They still live in the same city they lived in before but do not go back to stay the night in their village home and they take precautions if they visit their village.

Some have gone totally underground. Some went to home to their in-laws’ area and there are those who left the country and went into India. There are AL communities in Kolkata, Bangkok, Canada and the UK.

More students now go abroad but there has always been that trend. There are those who flee for refuge or economic reasons and those who are really at risk if they stay in the country. I don’t know how to determine those who are leaving for economic reasons and those who are at physical risk. There are some people who stayed in the country who would be at risk of harm. Grievances may come up, people might be vulnerable and police might not help. There are case backlogs, issues with gathering evidence and witnesses, and jail conditions are bad even if someone wants to surrender.

The former Speaker [of the National Parliament], Sharin Sharmin, had a case brought against her where there was no evidence and it was alleged that she shot someone elsewhere in the country. There are these weak, false cases brought against people. The situation is very complex, it is not simple.
